name: Anticholinergic toxidrome
oneLiner: Hot as a hare, blind as a bat, dry as a bone, red as a beet, mad as a hatter — and the bowel sounds are absent.

features.mentalStatus: agitation, delirium, hallucinations (often visual, lilliputian)

causativeAgents: antihistamines (diphenhydramine, chlorpheniramine, promethazine)
tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline, nortriptyline) — also Na-channel toxicity
antipsychotics (chlorpromazine, clozapine, olanzapine)
atropine, hyoscine (scopolamine), glycopyrrolate
oxybutynin, tolterodine (urinary antimuscarinics)
plants: Datura stramonium (jimsonweed), Atropa belladonna, Brugmansia
differentialDiagnosis: sympathomimetic toxidrome (skin is sweaty, bowel sounds present)
serotonin syndrome (clonus + hyperreflexia, history of serotonergic agent)
management: ABC, IV access, continuous cardiac monitoring, 12-lead ECG (TCA → wide QRS).
Cooling: undress, evaporative + tepid sponging; target core temp < 38.5°C.
IV fluid resuscitation (isotonic crystalloid) for hyperthermia / rhabdomyolysis prevention.
Benzodiazepines (lorazepam 1-2 mg IV titrated) for agitation — avoid antipsychotics (worsen anticholinergic load and lower seizure threshold).
Foley catheter for urinary retention if present.

Physostigmine 1-2 mg IV slowly (over 5 min) ONLY for pure anticholinergic delirium without TCA features and without ECG changes — contraindicated if QRS > 100 ms or any conduction delay. Discuss with toxicology first.
Sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mEq/kg IV bolus if TCA overdose with wide QRS.
Activated charcoal 1 g/kg PO/NG if presented within 1 hour AND airway protected.
antidote: Physostigmine 1-2 mg IV (adult) slowly — only in pure anticholinergic delirium with normal ECG; do not use if TCA suspected.
redFlags: QRS > 100 ms (TCA poisoning) — give sodium bicarbonate, urgent ICU.
Seizures — benzodiazepines first-line.
Core temp > 40°C — aggressive active cooling.
Rhabdomyolysis (CK rising, dark urine) — IV fluids + monitor K+ / renal function.

references.label: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11e — Anticholinergics
UK National Poisons Information Service / TOXBASE — anticholinergic poisoning

name: Cholinergic toxidrome (SLUDGE / DUMBELS)
oneLiner: Wet everywhere (SLUDGE: salivation, lacrimation, urination, diarrhoea, GI cramps, emesis) with fasciculations and miosis — think organophosphate.

features.mentalStatus: anxiety → confusion → coma in severe cases
other: garlic / petroleum odour on patient or clothing

causativeAgents: organophosphate pesticides (malathion, chlorpyrifos, parathion, dichlorvos)
carbamate pesticides (carbaryl, methomyl, propoxur) — usually milder, self-limiting
nerve agents (sarin, VX, novichok)
medicinal cholinergics overdose (pyridostigmine, neostigmine, donepezil, rivastigmine)
muscarinic mushrooms (Inocybe spp., Clitocybe spp.)
differentialDiagnosis: opioid overdose (also miosis + respiratory depression, but skin is dry and no fasciculations)
pontine stroke (miosis + coma but no SLUDGE)
management: PPE for staff — organophosphate is dermally absorbed; remove patient's clothing, wash skin with copious soap & water before extensive resuscitation.
ABC; high-flow O₂; suction copious secretions; early intubation if airway / ventilation compromised. AVOID succinylcholine (prolonged paralysis — pseudocholinesterase already inhibited).

Atropine 1-3 mg IV (adult) or 0.05 mg/kg (child) — DOUBLE the dose every 3-5 minutes until secretions dry and chest is clear; titrate to bronchorrhoea, NOT to pupil size or heart rate. May need very large cumulative doses (tens to hundreds of mg).

Pralidoxime (2-PAM) 30 mg/kg IV over 30 min (max 2 g), then 8-10 mg/kg/h infusion — give within 24-48 h of exposure, before ageing of the enzyme. Carbamate poisoning does not strictly require pralidoxime.
Benzodiazepines (diazepam 5-10 mg IV) for seizures and to reduce CNS toxicity.
Continuous cardiac monitoring; manage hypotension with IV fluids and noradrenaline if needed.
antidote: Atropine (titrated to dry secretions — primary endpoint is clear chest, not heart rate) PLUS pralidoxime (2-PAM) for organophosphates.
redFlags: Bronchorrhoea / bronchospasm — main cause of death; aggressive atropine.
Respiratory muscle weakness — anticipate intubation; AVOID suxamethonium.
Seizures or coma — benzodiazepines, ICU.
Type II (intermediate) syndrome 1-4 days post-exposure: proximal weakness, cranial nerve palsies → may need re-ventilation.

references.label: WHO. The WHO recommended classification of pesticides by hazard.
Eddleston M et al. Management of acute organophosphorus pesticide poisoning. Lancet 2008;371:597-607.

name: Opioid toxidrome
oneLiner: Triad: pinpoint pupils + respiratory depression + depressed mental status — reverse with naloxone, titrate to ventilation not consciousness.

features.respiratoryRate: bradypnoea (< 12) or apnoea — the lethal feature
features.pupils: miosis (pinpoint) — may be normal in meperidine, tramadol, propoxyphene, polypharmacy or anoxic injury
features.mentalStatus: somnolence, stupor, coma
other: track marks / patches / fentanyl analogue concerns

causativeAgents: heroin, fentanyl + analogues (carfentanil, nitazenes — extremely potent, may need repeat naloxone)
prescription opioids (morphine, oxycodone, hydromorphone, methadone, buprenorphine, tramadol)
loperamide (very high doses → QT prolongation + opioid features)
diphenoxylate-atropine (Lomotil — mixed opioid + anticholinergic features)
differentialDiagnosis: clonidine / imidazoline overdose (miosis + bradycardia, no rescue with naloxone)
organophosphate poisoning (also miosis, but wet and bradypnoeic with bronchorrhoea)
management: ABC — bag-mask ventilation with 100% O₂ first; this alone reverses most opioid deaths.

Naloxone 0.04-0.4 mg IV (adult, opioid-tolerant) or 0.4-2 mg IV/IM/intranasal in non-tolerant overdose. Titrate to adequate ventilation (RR ≥ 12, SpO₂ ≥ 92%), NOT to full alertness — over-reversal precipitates withdrawal, agitation, vomiting + aspiration.
Repeat naloxone every 2-3 min; if > 10 mg needed without response, reconsider diagnosis.
Naloxone infusion 2/3 of the effective bolus per hour for long-acting agents (methadone, sustained-release oxycodone, fentanyl patch, nitazenes).
IV fluids + supportive care; consider intubation if no response to naloxone or refractory hypoxia / NCPE.
Activated charcoal 1 g/kg PO/NG only if recent ingestion AND protected airway.
Refer to addiction services; consider buprenorphine induction if patient is willing and meets criteria. Distribute take-home naloxone.
antidote: Naloxone — see opioid-naloxone record for full dosing protocol.
redFlags: Pulmonary oedema / NCPE — supportive ventilation, PEEP.
QT prolongation (methadone) — continuous cardiac monitoring.
Body packer / stuffer — whole-bowel irrigation, surgical consult.
Polypharmacy (especially benzodiazepines / alcohol) — full naloxone reversal still leaves ventilatory depression; do not discharge prematurely.
Synthetic opioid (fentanyl analogue / nitazene) suspected — expect re-sedation, longer monitoring (≥ 6 h post last dose).

references.label: WHO. Community management of opioid overdose. 2014.
Boyer EW. Management of opioid analgesic overdose. NEJM 2012;367:146-55.

name: Sympathomimetic toxidrome
oneLiner: Hyperadrenergic state: hypertension + tachycardia + hyperthermia + mydriasis + diaphoresis + agitation — skin is sweaty, bowel sounds present (distinguishes from anticholinergic).

features.bloodPressure: hypertension (may be severe; risk of intracranial bleed, aortic dissection)
features.mentalStatus: agitation, paranoia, psychosis, hallucinations
features.bowelSounds: normal / hyperactive — KEY differentiator from anticholinergic (absent)

causativeAgents: cocaine (also Na-channel blockade → wide QRS)
amphetamines, methamphetamine, MDMA, MDPV (bath salts), cathinones
phenylpropanolamine, pseudoephedrine, ephedrine, phentermine
synthetic cannabinoids (variable presentation)
thyroid storm (clinical mimic — not a poisoning)
khat (Catha edulis) — cathinone-containing
differentialDiagnosis: anticholinergic toxidrome (dry skin, absent bowel sounds)
serotonin syndrome (clonus, hyperreflexia, history of serotonergic agent)
neuroleptic malignant syndrome (rigidity, history of antipsychotic exposure, slower onset)
management: ABC, continuous cardiac monitoring, 12-lead ECG, IV access, large-bore access for fluids.

Aggressive benzodiazepines (lorazepam 2-4 mg IV q5min titrated; or diazepam 5-10 mg IV q5min) — FIRST LINE for agitation, hypertension, tachycardia, seizures, and to lower body temperature indirectly. Cumulative doses often large.

Active cooling: undress, evaporative cooling, cool IV fluids; target core temp < 38.5°C within 30 min. Consider neuromuscular blockade + intubation + cooling if temp > 41°C refractory to benzodiazepines.
IV fluid resuscitation (isotonic crystalloid) for rhabdomyolysis prevention and hyperthermia.

Hypertension: titrate benzodiazepines first. If persistent, use vasodilator (phentolamine 1-5 mg IV; nitroglycerin or nicardipine infusion). AVOID pure β-blockers (esmolol, propranolol) in cocaine — historic concern of unopposed α-agonism; if β-blockade is required use a combined α/β agent (labetalol) only after α-blockade established.
Cocaine + chest pain: aspirin, nitroglycerin, benzodiazepines; if STEMI, primary PCI is preferred over thrombolysis.
Sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mEq/kg IV for QRS widening (cocaine Na-channel blockade).
antidote: No specific antidote. Benzodiazepines are the cornerstone of management.
redFlags: Core temp > 41°C — life-threatening; aggressive cooling + paralysis.
Wide QRS or ventricular arrhythmia (cocaine) — sodium bicarbonate.
Severe hypertension with end-organ damage — vasodilator, NOT pure β-blockade.
Chest pain — rule out MI / aortic dissection.
Seizures — benzodiazepines; if refractory, barbiturates or propofol.
Hyponatraemia (MDMA + free water) — careful sodium correction.

references.label: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11e — Cocaine; Amphetamines.
Richards JR et al. Treatment of cocaine cardiovascular toxicity. Clin Toxicol 2016.

name: Sedative-hypnotic toxidrome
oneLiner: CNS depression with relatively preserved vitals: somnolence + slurred speech + ataxia + nystagmus, normal pupils, normal-ish respirations (until severe).

features.respiratoryRate: normal early; bradypnoea in severe cases (especially with alcohol or opioid co-ingestion)
features.mentalStatus: drowsy → stupor → coma in overdose; ataxia, slurred speech, disinhibition
other: co-ingestion with alcohol is the main lethality multiplier

causativeAgents: benzodiazepines (diazepam, alprazolam, lorazepam, clonazepam, midazolam)
Z-drugs (zolpidem, zopiclone, eszopiclone)
barbiturates (phenobarbital, thiopental) — narrower therapeutic index, higher mortality
gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB) and precursors (GBL, 1,4-BD)
ethanol (the most common co-ingestant)
first-generation antihistamines (also anticholinergic)
carisoprodol, meprobamate
differentialDiagnosis: opioid toxidrome (miosis + bradypnoea; reverses with naloxone)
management: ABC, supplemental O₂, IV access, glucose check (POC + lab), continuous cardiac + pulse-oximetry monitoring.
Supportive care is the mainstay — most patients do well with airway protection and observation.
Bag-mask ventilation / intubation for inadequate ventilation, hypoxia, or loss of airway reflexes.
IV fluids for hypotension; vasopressors rarely needed.

Flumazenil 0.2 mg IV (then 0.3-0.5 mg q1min, max 3 mg) for ISOLATED iatrogenic benzodiazepine over-sedation in a benzodiazepine-naive patient. AVOID in chronic benzodiazepine users, mixed overdose (especially with TCAs), known seizure disorder — risk of refractory seizures.
Active rewarming if hypothermic.
Consider haemodialysis for severe phenobarbital or carbamazepine overdose.
Activated charcoal 1 g/kg if presented < 1 h AND airway protected.
antidote: Flumazenil — for isolated, iatrogenic benzodiazepine over-sedation only. Do NOT use empirically in mixed or chronic-user overdose.
redFlags: Mixed overdose with opioids, alcohol, or TCAs — disproportionate respiratory failure.
Severe barbiturate poisoning — coma, hypothermia, hypotension → ICU + consider haemodialysis (phenobarbital).
GHB overdose — abrupt awakening 2-4 h later; do not assume malingering.
Aspiration pneumonia.

references.label: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11e — Sedative-hypnotics.
Penninga EI et al. Adverse events associated with flumazenil treatment. BMC Pharmacol Toxicol 2016.

name: Serotonin syndrome
oneLiner: Triad: mental status change + autonomic hyperactivity + neuromuscular hyperactivity (clonus, hyperreflexia — LOWER-LIMB DOMINANT). Hunter Criteria > Sternbach.

features.mentalStatus: agitation, restlessness, confusion → coma in severe cases
other: clonus — spontaneous, inducible (ankle) or ocular — KEY finding

causativeAgents: SSRIs / SNRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline, paroxetine, citalopram, escitalopram, venlafaxine, duloxetine)
MAOIs (phenelzine, tranylcypromine, selegiline, moclobemide) — high-risk combinations
tramadol, tapentadol, meperidine, fentanyl, methadone, pethidine
ondansetron, metoclopramide, dextromethorphan, linezolid (also MAOI activity)
St John's wort, MDMA, cocaine, amphetamines, LSD
lithium, triptans (combined with SSRIs)
methylene blue (MAOI activity) given to a patient on SSRI
differentialDiagnosis: neuroleptic malignant syndrome (slow onset over days, lead-pipe rigidity, normo- or hyporeflexia, history of antipsychotic exposure)
management: Stop all serotonergic agents IMMEDIATELY — most cases resolve within 24 h once the offending agent is withdrawn.
ABC, continuous cardiac monitoring, IV access, IV fluids.
Aggressive cooling for hyperthermia: undress, evaporative cooling, IV crystalloid; target core temp < 38.5°C.
Benzodiazepines (lorazepam 1-2 mg IV q5min titrated; or diazepam) for agitation, tremor, clonus — first line. Cumulative doses often large.

Cyproheptadine PO/NG — 12 mg loading dose, then 2 mg q2h while symptoms persist, up to 8 mg q6h maintenance (max 32 mg/24 h). Limited evidence; reasonable in moderate-severe cases unresponsive to benzodiazepines. No IV form.

Severe / refractory hyperthermia (> 41°C) — intubation + non-depolarising neuromuscular blockade (rocuronium / vecuronium — AVOID succinylcholine, exacerbates hyperkalaemia from rhabdomyolysis) + active cooling + sedation.
Manage hypertension as for sympathomimetic; AVOID propranolol (long-acting, masks tachycardia which is a useful clinical marker).
Treat rhabdomyolysis (IV fluids), monitor renal function, K+, lactate, CK.
antidote: Cyproheptadine PO/NG (5-HT2A antagonist) — adjunct to benzodiazepines + supportive care in moderate-severe cases.
redFlags: Core temp > 41°C — life-threatening; intubation, paralysis, aggressive cooling.
Rigidity with rhabdomyolysis, AKI, DIC.
Seizures — benzodiazepines.
Recent linezolid or methylene blue exposure — high index of suspicion.
Mixed with MDMA — also risk hyponatraemia from free-water intake.

references.label: Boyer EW, Shannon M. The serotonin syndrome. NEJM 2005;352:1112-20.
Dunkley EJC et al. The Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria. QJM 2003;96:635-42.

name: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS)
oneLiner: Tetrad over hours-to-days: lead-pipe rigidity + hyperthermia + autonomic instability + altered mental status, after dopamine antagonist exposure or dopaminergic withdrawal.

features.mentalStatus: altered — agitation, mutism, catatonia, coma

causativeAgents: typical antipsychotics (haloperidol, fluphenazine, chlorpromazine) — highest risk
atypical antipsychotics (risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, aripiprazole, clozapine) — lower risk but possible
antiemetics with dopamine antagonism (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, droperidol)
abrupt withdrawal of dopaminergic agents (levodopa, amantadine, pramipexole) in Parkinson's patients — 'parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome'
lithium, tetrabenazine
differentialDiagnosis: serotonin syndrome (rapid onset, clonus + hyperreflexia, lower-limb dominant)
malignant hyperthermia (anaesthetic trigger; hypercarbia; succinylcholine / volatile anaesthetic)
management: STOP the offending dopamine antagonist immediately. If parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia, RESTART the withdrawn dopaminergic agent.
ABC, continuous cardiac monitoring, IV access, large-bore IV fluids — high-volume to support renal perfusion (myoglobinuric AKI risk).
Aggressive active cooling: undress, evaporative cooling, cool IV fluids; target core temp < 38.5°C.
Benzodiazepines (lorazepam 1-2 mg IV q4-6h) — first-line for agitation, mild-moderate cases.
Bromocriptine 2.5 mg PO/NG q6-8h titrated up to 5 mg q4-6h (max 40 mg/day) — dopamine agonist, restores dopaminergic tone. Onset 24-72 h.
Dantrolene 1-2.5 mg/kg IV q6h (max 10 mg/kg/day) — direct muscle relaxant; reserve for severe rigidity / hyperthermia. Beware hepatotoxicity.
Amantadine 100 mg PO/NG bd as alternative dopaminergic agent.
Severe / refractory — intubation + non-depolarising paralysis + ICU. ECT has been used for refractory NMS and lethal catatonia.
Monitor CK, K+, lactate, renal function, coags; treat rhabdomyolysis (IV fluids, ± urinary alkalinisation).
DVT prophylaxis early — high VTE risk from immobility + rigidity.
Avoid antipsychotic re-challenge for at least 2 weeks after recovery; if needed later, use a different class at the lowest effective dose.
antidote: Bromocriptine PO (dopamine agonist) + dantrolene IV (muscle relaxant) for moderate-severe disease, in addition to withdrawal of the offending agent.
redFlags: Core temp > 41°C — life-threatening, ICU.
Rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuric AKI — aggressive IV fluids, renal replacement if needed.
Severe rigidity — risk of compartment syndrome.
Aspiration, pulmonary embolism (immobility), DIC.
Recurrence on re-introduction of antipsychotic — wait ≥ 2 weeks and use a different class.

references.label: Strawn JR et al. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Am J Psychiatry 2007;164:870-6.
Berman BD. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: a review for neurohospitalists. Neurohospitalist 2011;1:41-7.

name: Salicylate toxicity
oneLiner: Mixed primary respiratory alkalosis + primary metabolic acidosis with tinnitus, hyperpnoea (Kussmaul-like), nausea, agitation, hyperthermia — even at therapeutic levels in chronic toxicity.

features.respiratoryRate: tachypnoea + hyperpnoea (deep) — drives the respiratory alkalosis
features.mentalStatus: agitation → confusion → coma in severe / chronic poisoning
features.bowelSounds: normal or hyperactive; nausea, vomiting, haematemesis
other: non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema in severe cases
anion-gap metabolic acidosis with concomitant respiratory alkalosis

causativeAgents: aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid)
topical methyl salicylate (oil of wintergreen, deep heat rubs) — 1 tsp = ~7 g aspirin equivalent; lethal in children
bismuth subsalicylate (Pepto-Bismol) — chronic, in children
salicylate-containing keratolytics (high concentration over large body surface area)
differentialDiagnosis: DKA (high anion gap, but glucose elevated and ketones present)
management: ABC, IV access, continuous cardiac + pulse-oximetry monitoring, serial salicylate levels (q2h until peak then q4h; consider extended-release / enteric-coated formulations may peak late).
Salicylate level (mg/dL) + ABG + electrolytes + glucose + renal/liver function + lactate + coagulation + CK.
Activated charcoal 1 g/kg PO/NG within 1-2 h of acute ingestion (multiple-dose may be considered for sustained-release / massive ingestion).
IV fluid resuscitation (D5W with potassium added once urine output established) — patients are profoundly dehydrated.

SODIUM BICARBONATE IV — 1-2 mEq/kg bolus, then infusion (150 mEq NaHCO₃ in 1 L D5W at 1.5-2 × maintenance) — target urine pH > 7.5 and serum pH 7.45-7.55. Maintains salicylate in ionised form (ion trapping), enhances renal excretion, reverses CNS acidosis.
POTASSIUM REPLETION is essential — hypokalaemia prevents urinary alkalinisation. Aim for K+ 4-4.5 mmol/L.
Glucose — give D50 boluses even if serum glucose normal (CNS hypoglycaemia despite normal serum levels).

HAEMODIALYSIS — indications include level > 100 mg/dL acute (> 90 in chronic), altered mental status, renal failure, severe acid-base disturbance, pulmonary or cerebral oedema, or refractory to alkalinisation.
antidote: No specific antidote. Treatment is alkalinisation (sodium bicarbonate + potassium repletion) and early haemodialysis for severe poisoning.
redFlags: Altered mental status — INDICATION FOR HAEMODIALYSIS regardless of level.
Salicylate level > 100 mg/dL (acute) or > 60-90 mg/dL (chronic, often more toxic at lower level).
Cerebral oedema, seizures, coma.

Non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema — supportive ventilation; mechanical ventilation is HIGH-RISK as iatrogenic respiratory acidosis worsens CNS salicylate uptake. If intubation unavoidable, ventilate to match the patient's pre-intubation minute ventilation (often very high), give NaHCO₃ first.
Co-ingestion (paracetamol common with aspirin combination products).
Chronic toxicity in elderly — often missed, presents as confusion / acidosis.

references.label: EXTRIP workgroup. Extracorporeal treatment for salicylate poisoning. Ann Emerg Med 2015;66:165-81.
Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11e — Salicylates.

name: Tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) overdose
oneLiner: Anticholinergic + α1-blockade + Na-channel blockade: wide QRS, terminal R in aVR, hypotension, seizures, coma. Sodium bicarbonate is the cornerstone — 1-2 mEq/kg IV bolus for QRS > 100 ms.

features.heartRate: sinus tachycardia early; wide-complex tachycardia / VT late
features.mentalStatus: agitation → confusion → coma; seizures common
other: terminal R wave in aVR > 3 mm and R/S > 0.7 — classic ECG

causativeAgents: amitriptyline, nortriptyline, imipramine, clomipramine, dosulepin (dothiepin), doxepin
carbamazepine (similar Na-channel toxicity)
diphenhydramine in massive overdose (Na-channel blockade)
cocaine (similar Na-channel blockade)
type Ia / Ic antiarrhythmics (quinidine, flecainide, propafenone) — share Na-channel toxicity
management: ABC, large-bore IV access, continuous cardiac monitoring, 12-lead ECG immediately + q1h.

SODIUM BICARBONATE 1-2 mEq/kg IV bolus for QRS > 100 ms, hypotension, or ventricular arrhythmia. Repeat boluses or start infusion (150 mEq NaHCO₃ in 1 L D5W at 250 mL/h, target arterial pH 7.50-7.55). Endpoint is QRS narrowing.
Hypertonic saline 3% has been used as adjunct when bicarbonate insufficient.
Activated charcoal 1 g/kg PO/NG if within 1-2 h of ingestion AND airway protected.
Benzodiazepines for seizures (lorazepam 1-2 mg IV; or diazepam) — AVOID phenytoin (Na-channel blocker, worsens TCA toxicity).
Hypotension: IV crystalloid; vasopressors if refractory (noradrenaline preferred for α1 agonism).
Refractory cardiotoxicity: intralipid emulsion 20% 1.5 mL/kg IV bolus then 0.25 mL/kg/min infusion (limited evidence; consider as rescue).
Refractory arrhythmias: lidocaine (class Ib — different binding kinetics from TCA), magnesium, ECMO / VA-bypass as last-resort.
Avoid: class Ia/Ic antiarrhythmics, β-blockers, calcium channel blockers, physostigmine (all worsen toxicity).
antidote: Sodium bicarbonate is the cornerstone — narrows QRS, raises serum pH and Na+, both of which counter TCA Na-channel blockade.
redFlags: QRS > 100 ms — give bicarbonate immediately.
Terminal R wave > 3 mm in aVR — high risk of seizure / arrhythmia.
Seizures — benzodiazepines; AVOID phenytoin.
Refractory hypotension / arrhythmia — consider intralipid, ECMO.
Coma + wide QRS — intubation, ICU.

references.label: Body R et al. Guidelines in Emergency Medicine Network (GEMNet): guideline for the management of tricyclic antidepressant overdose. Emerg Med J 2011;28:347-68.
Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11e — Cyclic Antidepressants.

name: Beta-blocker overdose
oneLiner: Bradycardia + AV block + hypotension + hypoglycaemia + bronchospasm + (sometimes) seizures with propranolol. High-dose insulin-euglycaemia therapy (HIET) is the modern cornerstone; glucagon historic.

features.respiratoryRate: bronchospasm in asthmatics; respiratory depression with propranolol (lipophilic)
features.mentalStatus: normal early; obtunded with severe hypotension or propranolol (CNS effect)

causativeAgents: propranolol (most lethal — lipophilic, CNS penetration, Na-channel blockade in massive OD)
metoprolol, atenolol, bisoprolol, carvedilol, labetalol, nebivolol
sotalol (also K-channel blockade — QT prolongation, torsades)
timolol eye drops (massive systemic absorption in children)
differentialDiagnosis: calcium channel blocker overdose (similar bradycardia + hypotension; CCB usually hyperglycaemic, BB usually hypoglycaemic)
management: ABC, continuous cardiac monitoring, 12-lead ECG, IV access, glucose check, transcutaneous pacing pads ON the patient.
Activated charcoal 1 g/kg PO/NG if within 1-2 h AND airway protected.
IV crystalloid 10-20 mL/kg for hypotension.
Atropine 0.5-1 mg IV q3-5min (often ineffective in severe overdose).
GLUCAGON 5-10 mg IV bolus (adult), repeat at 10 min; then infusion 2-5 mg/h. Pretreat with antiemetic (ondansetron) — glucagon causes vomiting.

HIGH-DOSE INSULIN-EUGLYCAEMIA THERAPY (HIET): regular insulin 1 unit/kg IV bolus + dextrose 0.5 g/kg bolus (if glucose < 13 mmol/L); then insulin 1 unit/kg/h infusion (titrate up to 10 units/kg/h), with D10 or D25 infusion to maintain euglycaemia (4-10 mmol/L). Monitor K+ closely (hypokalaemia common).
Vasopressors: noradrenaline first-line; adrenaline if combined α/β needed; vasopressin as adjunct.
Transcutaneous → transvenous pacing for refractory bradycardia.
Intralipid emulsion 20% 1.5 mL/kg IV bolus then 0.25 mL/kg/min for lipophilic agents (propranolol) refractory to other measures.
Sodium bicarbonate for wide QRS (propranolol Na-channel blockade).
Refractory shock: ECMO / VA-bypass — these toxidromes can resolve over days, ECMO bridges them.
Sotalol-induced torsades: magnesium 2 g IV, isoprenaline, overdrive pacing.
antidote: No specific antidote. High-dose insulin-euglycaemia therapy (HIET) is now considered the cornerstone (replacing glucagon-only protocols), with glucagon, calcium, vasopressors, intralipid, and ECMO as adjuncts.
redFlags: Wide QRS (propranolol) — Na-channel blockade; bicarbonate.
Seizures (propranolol) — benzodiazepines.
Refractory shock — HIET + vasopressors + consider ECMO / VA-bypass.
Torsades (sotalol) — magnesium, isoprenaline, overdrive pacing.
Hypoglycaemia — dextrose; check often.
Co-ingestion with CCB / digoxin — additive toxicity.

references.label: Engebretsen KM et al. High-dose insulin therapy in beta-blocker and calcium channel-blocker poisoning. Clin Toxicol 2011;49:277-83.
Graudins A et al. Calcium channel antagonist and beta-blocker overdose: antidotes and adjunct therapies. Br J Clin Pharmacol 2016;81:453-61.

name: Calcium channel blocker (CCB) overdose
oneLiner: Bradycardia + hypotension + HYPERGLYCAEMIA (BB usually hypoglycaemic; CCB usually hyperglycaemic — useful discriminator). HIET cornerstone; calcium, glucagon, intralipid adjuncts.

features.heartRate: bradycardia (verapamil, diltiazem) or reflex tachycardia (amlodipine — vasodilator predominant)
features.respiratoryRate: normal early; pulmonary oedema in severe cases
features.mentalStatus: normal early; obtunded with severe hypotension
other: HYPERGLYCAEMIA (insulin-release inhibition) — useful discriminator from BB

causativeAgents: non-dihydropyridines: verapamil, diltiazem (more cardiotoxic — bradycardia + AV block)
dihydropyridines: amlodipine, nifedipine, felodipine (more vasodilatory — reflex tachycardia, vasoplegia)
extended-release formulations: delayed peak 6-12 h after ingestion — anticipate late deterioration
differentialDiagnosis: beta-blocker overdose (hypoglycaemia favours BB; hyperglycaemia favours CCB)
management: ABC, continuous cardiac monitoring, 12-lead ECG, IV access, glucose check, transcutaneous pacing pads ON.
Activated charcoal 1 g/kg PO/NG if within 1-2 h; consider WHOLE-BOWEL IRRIGATION for sustained-release preparations (polyethylene glycol 1.5-2 L/h until rectal effluent clear).
IV crystalloid for hypotension.
Atropine 0.5-1 mg IV q3-5min (limited efficacy).
CALCIUM: calcium chloride 10% 10-20 mL IV (or calcium gluconate 10% 30-60 mL — less irritant peripherally), repeat q10min × 3-4 then infusion (0.2-0.4 mL/kg/h CaCl).
GLUCAGON 5-10 mg IV bolus, infusion 2-5 mg/h (less reliable than for BB).

HIGH-DOSE INSULIN-EUGLYCAEMIA THERAPY (HIET): regular insulin 1 unit/kg IV bolus (give dextrose first if glucose < 13 mmol/L), then 1 unit/kg/h titrated up to 10 unit/kg/h, with D10/D25 infusion to maintain euglycaemia, monitor K+. Cornerstone of modern care.
Vasopressors: noradrenaline first-line; vasopressin adjunct; adrenaline if combined β-stimulation helpful.
Intralipid emulsion 20% 1.5 mL/kg IV bolus + 0.25 mL/kg/min for lipophilic CCB (verapamil, diltiazem).
Methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg IV has been reported in refractory amlodipine vasoplegia (off-label, last-resort).
Refractory shock: ECMO / VA-bypass.
antidote: No specific antidote. HIET is the modern cornerstone; calcium + glucagon + vasopressors + intralipid + ECMO are adjuncts.
redFlags: Sustained-release ingestion — late deterioration; admit for ≥ 24 h monitoring.
Refractory shock — HIET, intralipid, vasopressors, ECMO.
Mixed BB + CCB ingestion — synergistic cardiotoxicity.
Hyperkalaemia from HIET-induced insulin shift — monitor K+ and replace.
Pulmonary oedema (amlodipine) — supportive ventilation.

references.label: St-Onge M et al. Experts consensus recommendations for the management of calcium channel blocker poisoning in adults. Crit Care Med 2017;45:e306-15.
Engebretsen KM et al. Clin Toxicol 2011.

name: Digoxin toxicity
oneLiner: Nausea + visual disturbance (yellow-green halos / xanthopsia) + bradyarrhythmias / ectopy + HYPERKALAEMIA (acute) — digoxin-specific Fab fragments for severe toxicity.

features.heartRate: bradycardia, AV block, or paradoxical tachy-arrhythmias (atrial tachycardia with block, junctional tachycardia, bidirectional VT — pathognomonic)
features.mentalStatus: confusion, delirium, hallucinations (especially elderly, chronic)
other: YELLOW-GREEN VISION / xanthopsia / halos — classic but not always present
HYPERKALAEMIA in acute toxicity (Na/K-ATPase inhibition) — strong predictor of mortality > 5.5 mmol/L pre-Fab era

causativeAgents: digoxin (prescription overdose / accumulation in renal impairment / drug interactions)
drug interactions: amiodarone, verapamil, quinidine, macrolides (clarithromycin, erythromycin), spironolactone — raise digoxin levels
natural cardiac glycosides: oleander (Nerium / Thevetia), foxglove (Digitalis), lily of the valley, toad venom (bufadienolides)
management: ABC, continuous cardiac monitoring, 12-lead ECG, IV access, K+ + Mg + renal function + digoxin level (drawn ≥ 6 h post-dose for accurate steady-state).
Activated charcoal 1 g/kg PO/NG if within 1-2 h AND airway protected (also useful in chronic toxicity if ongoing absorption suspected).

DIGOXIN-SPECIFIC ANTIBODY FRAGMENTS (Fab, DigiFab) — first-line for: life-threatening arrhythmia, K+ > 5 mmol/L in acute (> 5.5 historically), serum digoxin level > 15 ng/mL post-distribution OR > 10 ng/mL with symptoms, ingested dose > 10 mg (adult) or > 4 mg (child), chronic toxicity with arrhythmia in renal impairment. Empirical dosing acute ingestion: 10-20 vials; chronic: 3-6 vials initially. Or calculate by ingested mg or serum level (see DigiFab labelling).
Atropine 0.5-1 mg IV for bradycardia.
Transcutaneous → transvenous pacing for refractory bradycardia (but risk arrhythmia provocation).
Magnesium 2 g IV for ventricular ectopy / arrhythmia.

AVOID calcium for hyperkalaemia in digoxin toxicity — historic concern of 'stone heart' (precipitating fatal arrhythmia); insulin-dextrose, sodium bicarbonate, salbutamol preferred; Fab definitively treats both arrhythmia and hyperkalaemia.
AVOID class Ia / Ic antiarrhythmics; phenytoin / lidocaine have been used for ventricular arrhythmia.
Haemodialysis is NOT effective for digoxin (large Vd, tissue-bound) — useful only for hyperkalaemia management if Fab unavailable.
antidote: Digoxin-specific antibody fragments (DigiFab / Digibind) — definitive antidote; reverses arrhythmia and hyperkalaemia within 30 min.
redFlags: K+ > 5 mmol/L in acute toxicity — strong mortality predictor; give Fab.
Bidirectional VT — pathognomonic; give Fab.
Renal impairment + chronic toxicity — Fab with reduced threshold.
Avoid calcium for hyperkalaemia in digoxin toxicity (relative contraindication).
Plant cardiac glycoside exposure (oleander) — Fab cross-reactivity is variable; higher doses often needed.

references.label: Hack JB, Lewin NA. Cardioactive steroids. In: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11e.
Roberts DM et al. The clinical pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics and clinical effectiveness of digoxin-specific antibody fragments. Clin Pharmacokinet 2016;55:1209-25.

name: Lithium toxicity
oneLiner: Tremor + ataxia + dysarthria + confusion + fasciculations → seizures + coma in severe cases. GI symptoms early in acute; neurologic dominant in chronic. Haemodialysis for severe / chronic toxicity.

features.heartRate: normal or bradycardia; QT prolongation, T-wave flattening
features.mentalStatus: tremor → ataxia → dysarthria → confusion → seizures → coma
features.bowelSounds: hyperactive in acute (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea); normal in chronic
other: coarse tremor, hyperreflexia, clonus, fasciculations, myoclonus
SILENT (Syndrome of Irreversible Lithium-Effectuated NeuroToxicity) — persistent neurologic deficit

causativeAgents: lithium carbonate (Camcolit, Priadel, Lithobid) — prescription
acute-on-chronic: dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE-inhibitors, thiazides, renal impairment — all reduce lithium clearance
intentional acute overdose
differentialDiagnosis: serotonin syndrome (clonus, hyperreflexia — but also from lithium + SSRI combination)
management: ABC, IV access, continuous cardiac monitoring, 12-lead ECG, glucose check, lithium level (peak 2-4 h acute IR; consider repeat to monitor).
IV fluid resuscitation with isotonic saline — promotes renal excretion; aim for high-normal urine output. Avoid hypotonic fluids (sodium-paired excretion).
Activated charcoal does NOT bind lithium — DO NOT give for lithium alone (consider polyethylene glycol whole-bowel irrigation for sustained-release ingestion).
Sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Kayexalate) — historical adjunct; not first-line.

HAEMODIALYSIS — strongly indicated for: severe neurologic symptoms (seizures, coma) regardless of level, level > 4 mEq/L acute, level > 2.5 mEq/L chronic or with renal impairment or symptoms refractory to fluids, level > 5 mEq/L absolute, inability to tolerate IV fluids (renal / cardiac failure). Re-dialyse if rebound occurs (intracellular lithium redistributes).
Continuous renal replacement therapy (CVVHDF) as alternative if haemodynamically unstable.
Seizures: benzodiazepines first-line.
Stop lithium; review precipitants (dehydration, drug interactions, renal function).
Long-term neurologic sequelae (SILENT) — neurology / rehab review post-discharge.
antidote: No specific antidote. Aggressive IV crystalloid + early haemodialysis are definitive.
redFlags: Severe neurologic symptoms (coma, seizures) — dialysis regardless of level.
Level > 4 mEq/L acute or > 2.5 mEq/L chronic — dialysis indication.
Renal impairment — early dialysis (cannot rely on renal clearance).
Rebound rise after dialysis (intracellular redistribution) — repeat level at 6-12 h; redialyse if needed.
SILENT — persistent cerebellar / extrapyramidal deficit despite normal levels.

references.label: Decker BS et al. EXTRIP workgroup recommendations on extracorporeal treatment for lithium poisoning. Clin J Am Soc Nephrol 2015;10:875-87.
Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11e — Lithium.

name: Iron toxicity (paediatric ingestion the classic)
oneLiner: Five phases: GI (0-6 h vomiting + bloody diarrhoea) → quiescent (6-24 h, falsely reassuring) → shock + metabolic acidosis (12-48 h) → hepatic failure (48-96 h) → late GI strictures. Desferrioxamine for severe toxicity.

features.skin: pale, mottled in shock; jaundice late
features.mentalStatus: irritable → lethargic → coma
features.bowelSounds: early: vomiting, haematemesis, bloody diarrhoea (corrosive); late: stricture / obstruction (4-6 weeks)
other: RADIO-OPAQUE TABLETS ON ABDOMINAL X-RAY (helpful but not universal — chewables / paediatric forms often invisible)

causativeAgents: ferrous sulfate, fumarate, gluconate (prenatal vitamins, supplements)
paediatric chewable iron supplements (sweet-tasting, high-dose)
polysaccharide-iron complex (lower toxicity)
differentialDiagnosis: salicylate / paracetamol overdose (also anion gap, hepatic)
viral gastroenteritis (children — but stable, no metabolic acidosis)
management: ABC, IV access (large-bore for shock), continuous cardiac monitoring, glucose check.
Serum iron level at 4 h (acute) and 8 h (sustained-release) post-ingestion. TIBC has no role.
Abdominal X-ray to look for radio-opaque tablets — guides decontamination.
Whole-bowel irrigation with polyethylene glycol 1.5-2 L/h until rectal effluent clear if tablets visible on X-ray or massive ingestion. ACTIVATED CHARCOAL DOES NOT BIND IRON — do not give.
Aggressive IV crystalloid resuscitation for shock (often L of fluid required in children).
Correct metabolic acidosis with fluid + occasionally bicarbonate; do not over-correct (alkalosis worsens iron precipitation).

DESFERRIOXAMINE (deferoxamine) IV 15 mg/kg/h, max 6 g/24 h (standard) — chelates free iron; produces vin rosé urine indicating active chelation. Indications: serum iron > 90 µmol/L (500 µg/dL) at 4-6 h, ANY symptoms with serum iron 60-90 µmol/L, severe systemic toxicity regardless of level, persistent metabolic acidosis, shock. Continue until symptoms resolve and urine colour normalises (usually 12-24 h).
Watch for ARDS with prolonged desferrioxamine use (> 24 h) and Yersinia sepsis (desferrioxamine promotes Yersinia growth).
Hepatology referral if hepatic failure develops.
Endoscopy at 4-6 weeks for stricture surveillance if severe corrosive injury.
antidote: Desferrioxamine IV — chelates free iron, urinary excretion (urine vin rosé).
redFlags: Children — peak fatality age 1-3 y; assume serious until proven otherwise.
Serum iron > 90 µmol/L — desferrioxamine.
Persistent metabolic acidosis / shock — desferrioxamine regardless of level.
Quiescent phase (6-24 h) is falsely reassuring — anticipate phase 3 deterioration.
Hepatic failure (phase 4) — high mortality without transplant.
Late GI stricture / obstruction (4-6 weeks) — surveillance.

references.label: Tenenbein M. Position statement: ipecac syrup. Clin Toxicol 2004 (now withdrawn for iron).
Manoguerra AS et al. Iron ingestion: an evidence-based consensus guideline for out-of-hospital management. Clin Toxicol 2005;43:553-70.

name: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose
oneLiner: Four phases: I (0-24 h asymptomatic / mild nausea) → II (24-72 h transaminitis, RUQ pain, may feel better) → III (72-96 h fulminant hepatic failure) → IV (recovery or transplant). N-acetylcysteine if Rumack-Matthew nomogram in toxic range or staggered ingestion / late presentation.

features.heartRate: normal early; tachycardia with hepatic failure
features.respiratoryRate: normal early; Kussmaul with metabolic acidosis late
features.mentalStatus: alert early; hepatic encephalopathy phase III-IV
features.bowelSounds: nausea, vomiting; RUQ tenderness phase II
other: INITIALLY ASYMPTOMATIC — major pitfall; do not be reassured
INR ↑ phase II-III (marker of synthetic failure)
renal failure (often co-occurs with hepatic in severe)
lactic acidosis (early massive ingestion or late hepatic failure)

causativeAgents: paracetamol / acetaminophen — single-ingredient (Panadol, Tylenol)
combination products — co-codamol, cold/flu remedies, Vicodin, Percocet (paracetamol + opioid)
topical / rectal paracetamol — possible in massive doses
chronic supratherapeutic (4 g+/day) in malnourished / alcoholic / fasting / CYP2E1 induced — toxic at lower doses
management: ABC, IV access, glucose check, full panel: paracetamol level at 4 h post-ingestion (or as late as feasible), ALT/AST, INR, U&E, ABG, lactate, FBC.
Activated charcoal 1 g/kg PO/NG within 1-2 h of ingestion (some centres extend to 4 h for very large ingestions).
PLOT 4 h LEVEL ON RUMACK-MATTHEW NOMOGRAM: if above the treatment line (varies by jurisdiction — UK 100 mg/L at 4 h; US 150 mg/L at 4 h — UK lowered post-MHRA 2012), give N-acetylcysteine.

NAC IV: 150 mg/kg over 1 h + 50 mg/kg over 4 h + 100 mg/kg over 16 h (total 300 mg/kg over 21 h) — standard regimen. OR a 2-bag simplified regimen (200 mg/kg over 4 h + 100 mg/kg over 16 h) reduces anaphylactoid reactions. PO NAC 140 mg/kg loading + 70 mg/kg q4h × 17 doses is an alternative (poorer tolerance).
STAGGERED / LATE PRESENTATION (> 8 h) / UNKNOWN TIME: give NAC empirically without waiting for level — nomogram less reliable.
Continue NAC beyond standard duration if INR > 2.0 or ALT rising — until INR < 2 and ALT trending down.
Manage anaphylactoid reactions (5-15% with IV NAC): slow infusion rate, give antihistamine, hydrocortisone; continue NAC.

King's College Criteria for transplant referral (acute liver failure on paracetamol): pH < 7.30 OR (INR > 6.5 + creatinine > 300 µmol/L + grade III/IV encephalopathy). Refer to hepatology / transplant centre EARLY (within hours, not days).
Supportive: glucose for hypoglycaemia, FFP if invasive procedures (do not pre-empt unless bleeding — INR is a transplant-decision biomarker), renal support if AKI.
antidote: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) — replenishes glutathione, scavenges NAPQI metabolite. IV regimen standard; effective if started within 8 h of acute ingestion (ideally) but beneficial up to 24 h+ in late presentations.
redFlags: Initial asymptomatic phase is misleading — always check 4-h level.
Staggered ingestion / unknown time / chronic supratherapeutic — give NAC empirically.
Worsening INR / encephalopathy → King's College Criteria → transplant referral EARLY.
Co-ingestion (TCA, salicylate) common — screen broadly.
Massive ingestion + lactic acidosis early — extra-hepatic mitochondrial toxicity; may need higher NAC and earlier transplant referral.

references.label: MHRA paracetamol overdose treatment guidance (UK, 2012) — single 100 mg/L treatment line.
Heard KJ. Acetylcysteine for acetaminophen poisoning. NEJM 2008;359:285-92.

name: Methanol toxicity
oneLiner: High anion gap metabolic acidosis + OSMOLAR GAP + visual disturbance (snowstorm vision, blindness) after illicit / contaminated alcohol. Fomepizole or ethanol blocks ADH; haemodialysis for severe toxicity.

features.pupils: dilated, reactive; later non-reactive in severe blindness
features.mentalStatus: drunken appearance early (mild); coma late
other: VISUAL DISTURBANCE — blurring, central scotomas, snowstorm vision, photophobia, blindness
OSMOLAR GAP early (parent compound); ANION GAP late (formic acid metabolite)
fundoscopy: optic disc hyperaemia early, pallor late

causativeAgents: windscreen washer fluid, antifreeze (some), denatured alcohol, illicit moonshine / counterfeit spirits
fuel-grade alcohol
industrial solvents (paint thinners, gum-removers)
differentialDiagnosis: ethylene glycol (similar mechanism; calcium oxalate crystals in urine, renal failure)
ethanol intoxication (no severe acidosis at low-moderate levels)
management: ABC, IV access, continuous cardiac monitoring, glucose check, full panel: ABG, electrolytes, urea, creatinine, glucose, lactate, methanol and ethanol levels, osmolality (measured + calculated, gap > 10-25 suggests toxic alcohol).
FOMEPIZOLE 15 mg/kg IV loading, then 10 mg/kg q12h × 4 doses, then 15 mg/kg q12h. First-line; inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase → prevents conversion to formic acid. Adjust dose if dialysing.
ETHANOL infusion as alternative if fomepizole unavailable — target serum ethanol 100-150 mg/dL (22-33 mmol/L); loading 0.6-0.8 g/kg IV then maintenance 80-150 mg/kg/h (higher if chronic alcoholic).
FOLINIC ACID (leucovorin) 1-2 mg/kg IV q4-6h — promotes folate-dependent conversion of formic acid to CO₂ + water.
SODIUM BICARBONATE 1-2 mEq/kg IV bolus then infusion for severe acidosis (pH < 7.3) — also slows formic acid retinal uptake.

HAEMODIALYSIS — indications: methanol level > 50 mg/dL (15.6 mmol/L), severe metabolic acidosis (pH < 7.15 or HCO3 < 15 despite bicarb), visual disturbance / blindness, renal failure, refractory haemodynamic instability. Continue until methanol level < 20-25 mg/dL AND acidosis corrected.
Continue fomepizole / ethanol therapy throughout dialysis (drug is removed; dose-adjust).
Ophthalmology consult — visual recovery may be partial / incomplete despite treatment.
antidote: Fomepizole (4-methylpyrazole) — competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase. Ethanol as alternative. Folinic acid to enhance formic acid metabolism. Haemodialysis definitively removes drug.
redFlags: Visual symptoms — irreversible blindness possible despite treatment; expedite fomepizole + dialysis.
Methanol level > 50 mg/dL — dialysis.
Severe acidosis (pH < 7.15) — dialysis + bicarbonate.
Co-ingested ethanol initially protective (substrate competition) — does NOT reduce ultimate toxicity, only delays it.
Delayed presentation (chronic moonshine) — patients may have advanced injury at presentation.

references.label: Roberts DM et al. Recommendations for the role of extracorporeal treatments in the management of acute methanol poisoning. Crit Care Med 2015;43:461-72.
Brent J. Fomepizole for ethylene glycol and methanol poisoning. NEJM 2009;360:2216-23.

name: Ethylene glycol toxicity
oneLiner: High anion gap metabolic acidosis + OSMOLAR GAP + CALCIUM OXALATE CRYSTALS in urine + renal failure ± neurologic depression. Fomepizole + thiamine + pyridoxine; haemodialysis for severe.

features.mentalStatus: drunken early (Stage 1, 0-12 h) → cardiopulmonary (Stage 2, 12-24 h) → renal (Stage 3, 24-72 h)
other: URINE FLUORESCENCE under Wood's lamp (fluorescein dye in commercial antifreeze) — useful early
CALCIUM OXALATE CRYSTALS (envelope-shaped monohydrate; needle-shaped dihydrate) in urine sediment
HYPOCALCAEMIA from oxalate chelation — tetany, QT prolongation, seizures
ANION GAP + OSMOLAR GAP early; gap closes as ethylene glycol metabolised

causativeAgents: antifreeze (radiator coolant) — sweet taste, attractive to children + animals
brake fluid, hydraulic fluid
industrial solvents
differentialDiagnosis: methanol (visual symptoms; no renal failure; no oxalate crystals)
management: ABC, IV access, continuous cardiac monitoring, glucose check, full panel: ABG, electrolytes, ionised calcium, urea, creatinine, glucose, lactate, ethylene glycol + ethanol levels, osmolality, urine microscopy (oxalate crystals), Wood's lamp on urine.
FOMEPIZOLE 15 mg/kg IV loading, then 10 mg/kg q12h × 4 doses, then 15 mg/kg q12h — first-line (preferred over ethanol).
ETHANOL infusion if fomepizole unavailable — target 100-150 mg/dL.
THIAMINE 100 mg IV daily — promotes shunt of glyoxylic acid metabolite to non-toxic α-hydroxy-β-ketoadipate.
PYRIDOXINE (vitamin B6) 100 mg IV daily — promotes shunt to glycine (less toxic).
CALCIUM REPLACEMENT for symptomatic hypocalcaemia (avoid prophylactic — may precipitate oxalate in tissues): calcium gluconate 10% 10-20 mL IV slowly.
SODIUM BICARBONATE 1-2 mEq/kg IV bolus for severe acidosis.

HAEMODIALYSIS — indications: ethylene glycol level > 50 mg/dL (8.1 mmol/L), severe acidosis (pH < 7.3), renal failure, end-organ damage. Continue until level < 20 mg/dL and acidosis resolved. Fomepizole therapy continues throughout dialysis with dose adjustment (q4h instead of q12h).
Renal recovery may be slow — RRT often needed for days-weeks.
Volume resuscitation to support renal perfusion + dilute oxalate crystals.
antidote: Fomepizole + thiamine + pyridoxine + (selective) calcium. Ethanol as alternative if fomepizole unavailable. Haemodialysis definitive in severe cases.
redFlags: Renal failure — early dialysis even at lower ethylene glycol levels.
Severe acidosis (pH < 7.15) — dialysis.
Hypocalcaemia with QT prolongation / seizures — calcium replacement.
Coingestion with other alcohols / drugs.
Paediatric ingestion — sweet antifreeze appealing; calculate dose carefully.

references.label: Brent J. Fomepizole for ethylene glycol and methanol poisoning. NEJM 2009;360:2216-23.
Ghannoum M et al. Extracorporeal treatment for ethylene glycol poisoning: EXTRIP recommendations. Crit Care Med 2018.

name: Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning
oneLiner: Headache + nausea + dizziness + confusion + (sometimes) cherry-red skin (unreliable). Pulse oximetry FALSELY NORMAL. Diagnose by carboxyhaemoglobin (COHb) co-oximetry. 100% O₂ via tight-fitting mask; hyperbaric for severe.

features.skin: Classically cherry-red but unreliable — most CO patients are pale or cyanotic
features.mentalStatus: headache → confusion → coma; delayed neuropsychiatric sequelae (DNS) weeks later
other: SpO₂ FALSELY NORMAL (pulse oximetry cannot distinguish COHb from O₂Hb) — measure COHb by co-oximetry

causativeAgents: house fire / smoke inhalation
poorly vented heating: gas / oil / wood / charcoal indoors, generators in garages
car exhaust (intentional / accidental in enclosed spaces)
industrial: coke ovens, blast furnaces
methylene chloride (paint stripper) — metabolised to CO; delayed peak
differentialDiagnosis: viral illness (winter — heating-related CO often misattributed)
management: ABC, remove from source, high-flow O₂ via tight-fitting non-rebreather mask immediately (do NOT wait for ABG / COHb).
Co-oximetry: arterial or venous blood gas with co-oximeter for COHb level (pulse oximetry cannot distinguish).
Full panel: ABG with lactate, electrolytes, troponin, ECG, CK, pregnancy test (impacts dispo).
100% NORMOBARIC O₂ until COHb < 5% AND symptom-free for ≥ 4 h (half-life on RA ~ 4-5 h; on 100% O₂ ~ 60-90 min).

HYPERBARIC OXYGEN (HBO) — consider if available within 6 h for: loss of consciousness at any time, neurologic deficit, abnormal cerebellar / cognitive examination, troponin / ECG evidence of myocardial ischaemia, pregnancy + COHb > 15-20% or any maternal symptom, COHb > 25% (some centres), severe acidosis. Evidence base is contested but reasonable in severe cases.
Treat coexisting cyanide poisoning in fire victims (see cyanide-poisoning record).
Treat shock with crystalloid + vasopressors.
Consider non-invasive ventilation / intubation if airway compromised.
Refer back to environment / occupational health to identify and remediate CO source — prevent re-exposure of patient + family.
Warn patient about Delayed Neuropsychiatric Sequelae (DNS): cognitive impairment, parkinsonism, mood disorder appearing 2-40 days after recovery — neurology follow-up.
antidote: 100% oxygen (normobaric or hyperbaric) — displaces CO from haemoglobin. No drug antidote.
redFlags: Loss of consciousness, neurologic deficit — HBO consideration.
Pregnancy — fetal Hb has higher CO affinity; HBO at lower threshold.
Pulse oximetry is FALSELY NORMAL — order COHb explicitly.
Smoke inhalation — consider cyanide co-poisoning; check lactate.
Children — more susceptible; lower threshold for HBO.
Delayed neuropsychiatric sequelae — warn patient, neurology follow-up.

references.label: Buckley NA et al. Hyperbaric oxygen for carbon monoxide poisoning. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2011.
Hampson NB et al. Practice recommendations in the diagnosis, management, and prevention of carbon monoxide poisoning. Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2012;186:1095-101.

name: Cyanide poisoning (smoke inhalation / industrial)
oneLiner: Tachypnoea → bradypnoea, coma, seizures, profound LACTIC ACIDOSIS in fire victim. Bitter almond breath (only ~ 60% of people perceive it). Hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV is first-line in suspected smoke-inhalation cyanide.

features.skin: cherry-red (venous SO₂ very high — cells cannot extract O₂) — but not always; cyanosis in late phase
features.mentalStatus: agitation → seizures → coma within minutes of significant exposure
other: PROFOUND LACTIC ACIDOSIS (> 10 mmol/L in fire victim) — KEY clue
narrowed arteriovenous O₂ difference (cells cannot use O₂)
bitter almond odour on breath (60% genetic perception)
soot in airway / face / sputum in fire victim

causativeAgents: smoke inhalation (especially burning plastics, wool, silk, polyurethane) — co-exists with CO
industrial: electroplating, jewellery manufacture, plastics, fumigation (hydrogen cyanide)
amygdalin-containing seeds / kernels (apricot, bitter almond, cassava — chronic / dietary)
sodium nitroprusside infusion (prolonged / high-dose)
intentional / suicidal ingestion
differentialDiagnosis: CO poisoning (often coexists in smoke inhalation)
hydrogen sulfide poisoning (similar mechanism, also fire / sewage)
management: ABC, 100% O₂ via non-rebreather, large-bore IV access, continuous monitoring, ECG, full panel: ABG with lactate, COHb, electrolytes, glucose, renal function.
DECONTAMINATION: remove from source, remove contaminated clothing — protect staff (especially with HCN gas).

HYDROXOCOBALAMIN (Cyanokit) 5 g IV over 15 min (repeatable to 10 g total) — first-line, especially in smoke inhalation. Binds cyanide → cyanocobalamin (vitamin B12), renally excreted. Side effects: red-orange skin / urine discoloration, interferes with colorimetric labs (haemodialysis machines, urine drug screens, CK assay), transient hypertension. Acceptable in pregnancy.
SODIUM THIOSULFATE 12.5 g IV (50 mL of 25% solution) over 10 min — donates sulfur to rhodanese enzyme → thiocyanate, renally excreted. Adjunct or alternative.

CYANIDE ANTIDOTE KIT (sodium nitrite + sodium thiosulfate) — older / US alternative. Sodium nitrite 300 mg IV induces methaemoglobinaemia (binds cyanide) — AVOID in smoke inhalation (CO already impairs O₂ delivery; methaemoglobinaemia worsens hypoxia).
Manage CO co-poisoning (see CO record): 100% O₂, consider HBO.
Manage acidosis with bicarbonate + IV fluids.
Seizures: benzodiazepines.
Refractory shock: vasopressors, ECMO.
Late: methaemoglobinaemia + sulfaemoglobinaemia from antidote can persist.
antidote: Hydroxocobalamin IV (Cyanokit) — first-line, especially in smoke inhalation. Sodium thiosulfate as adjunct or alternative. Avoid sodium nitrite in fire victims (worsens O₂ delivery).
redFlags: Fire victim + lactate > 10 mmol/L + altered mental status — give hydroxocobalamin empirically, do not wait for cyanide level (turnaround too slow).
Co-existing CO — manage simultaneously.
Hypotension / cardiac arrest — empirical hydroxocobalamin.
Avoid sodium nitrite if smoke inhalation (CO + methaemoglobinaemia = worse hypoxia).
Hydroxocobalamin interferes with labs / dialysis machines — alert lab + dialysis team.

references.label: Borron SW et al. Prospective study of hydroxocobalamin for acute cyanide poisoning in smoke inhalation. Ann Emerg Med 2007;49:794-801.
Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11e — Cyanide and Hydrogen Sulfide.

name: Carbamate / pyrethroid pesticide toxicity
oneLiner: Carbamate: short-acting reversible cholinergic — atropine yes, pralidoxime usually not. Pyrethroid: paraesthesia + agitation + sometimes seizures, mostly supportive; rarely life-threatening unless massive ingestion.

features.respiratoryRate: tachypnoea with bronchorrhoea in carbamate; normal in pyrethroid
features.mentalStatus: anxiety, confusion (carbamate); agitation, occasional seizures (pyrethroid, esp. type II)
other: carbamate effect resolves within hours (vs OP days)
pyrethroid: paraesthesia of face / extremities — KEY clue
type II pyrethroids (cyhalothrin, deltamethrin, cyano group) can cause seizures

causativeAgents: carbamates: carbaryl, methomyl, propoxur, aldicarb, carbofuran
pyrethroids type I: permethrin, allethrin, resmethrin (mild)
pyrethroids type II: cypermethrin, deltamethrin, cyhalothrin, fenvalerate (alpha-cyano group; potentially neurotoxic)
household insect sprays, head-lice / scabies treatments, agricultural
differentialDiagnosis: organophosphate (cholinergic) — more severe, longer-lasting; treat with pralidoxime (carbamate often does not need it)
management: PPE, decontamination: remove clothing, wash skin (both classes are dermally absorbed).

Carbamate: ABC, atropine 1-3 mg IV titrated to bronchorrhoea (same titration as for OP). PRALIDOXIME IS NOT ROUTINELY GIVEN — carbamate-cholinesterase bond spontaneously hydrolyses within hours and pralidoxime use is controversial / theoretically can worsen. Activated charcoal within 1 h. Most carbamate poisoning resolves in 24-48 h with supportive care.

Pyrethroid: ABC, antihistamines for urticaria, vitamin E oil or oily skin lotion for paraesthesia, benzodiazepines for agitation / seizures (rare). Activated charcoal if massive oral ingestion. No specific antidote.
Continuous cardiac monitoring in moderate-severe poisoning.
Seizures (pyrethroid type II): benzodiazepines first-line; phenytoin / levetiracetam if refractory.
AVOID atropine in pure pyrethroid poisoning (no cholinergic features).
antidote: Carbamate: atropine titrated to dry chest (NOT to heart rate); pralidoxime usually not indicated. Pyrethroid: no specific antidote — supportive.
redFlags: Mistaken identity — confirm carbamate vs organophosphate (OP needs pralidoxime).
Massive oral ingestion of pyrethroid — seizures possible; ICU.
Anaphylaxis-like presentation in pyrethroid — treat as anaphylaxis if hypotension / bronchospasm.
Co-exposure to OP + carbamate + solvent in commercial pesticide products.

references.label: Ramirez JA et al. Acute carbamate poisoning. In: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11e.
Bradberry SM et al. Poisoning due to pyrethroids. Toxicol Rev 2005;24:93-106.

name: Mushroom toxidromes (amatoxin, gyromitra, muscarinic, psychoactive)
oneLiner: AMATOXIN (Amanita phalloides) is the killer: delayed (6-24 h) severe GI then hepatic failure. Early-onset GI symptoms (< 6 h) usually milder. Gyromitra: seizures + hepatic injury — pyridoxine. Muscarinic mushrooms: cholinergic — atropine. Psychoactive: supportive.

features.pupils: variable (miosis with muscarinic; mydriasis with psychoactive / ibotenic)
features.mentalStatus: AMATOXIN — alert early then hepatic encephalopathy. GYROMITRA — seizures. MUSCARINIC — anxious then somnolent. PSYCHOACTIVE (psilocybin, Amanita muscaria) — hallucinations, agitation. ORELLANINE — renal-only, asymptomatic 2-14 days then renal failure.
features.bowelSounds: AMATOXIN — severe vomiting / cholera-like diarrhoea 6-24 h post-ingestion. MUSCARINIC — hyperactive. Others variable.
other: TIME-OF-ONSET is the most useful clinical discriminator: < 6 h = generally mild; > 6 h = consider amatoxin / gyromitra / orellanine — POTENTIALLY LETHAL

causativeAgents: AMATOXIN: Amanita phalloides (death cap), Amanita virosa, Galerina spp. — α-amanitin RNA polymerase II inhibitor
GYROMITRA / FALSE MOREL: Gyromitra esculenta — gyromitrin → monomethylhydrazine → seizures + hepatotoxicity (similar to isoniazid)
MUSCARINIC: Inocybe spp., Clitocybe dealbata — muscarine
PSYCHOACTIVE: Psilocybe / Panaeolus (psilocybin), Amanita muscaria / pantherina (ibotenic acid / muscimol — GABAergic + mild anticholinergic)
ORELLANINE: Cortinarius orellanus — delayed renal failure
COPRINUS: Coprinus atramentarius — disulfiram-like (with alcohol)
GI-IRRITANT: Chlorophyllum molybdites, Omphalotus illudens — early-onset, self-limiting
differentialDiagnosis: viral gastroenteritis (early-onset GI mushroom symptoms can mimic)
management: ABC, IV access, glucose, ALT/AST, INR, U&E, ABG, lactate, FBC, paracetamol level (always co-screen).
TIME OF SYMPTOM ONSET IS CRITICAL: < 6 h post-ingestion = usually less severe; > 6 h = high suspicion for amatoxin / gyromitra / orellanine.

AMATOXIN: aggressive IV fluids, activated charcoal (multiple-dose), N-acetylcysteine (as for paracetamol — empiric), silibinin / silymarin IV 5 mg/kg over 1 h then 20 mg/kg/day infusion (where available; chemoprotective vs amatoxin uptake into hepatocytes), high-dose penicillin G 1 million IU/kg/day (limited evidence, second-line), early transplant referral if INR > 2 / encephalopathy.
GYROMITRA: PYRIDOXINE 25 mg/kg IV (max 5 g) for seizures (similar to isoniazid toxidrome). Benzodiazepines. Hepatic supportive care.
MUSCARINIC: atropine 0.5-1 mg IV repeated to dry secretions (much lower doses than for OP).
PSYCHOACTIVE: supportive care, quiet environment, benzodiazepines if agitated.
ORELLANINE: aggressive IV fluids, anticipate AKI 2-14 days post-ingestion — nephrology referral; haemodialysis may be needed long-term.
Mycology / poison centre consultation to identify mushroom species — photograph + uneaten specimens.
Liver transplant centre referral early for amatoxin with INR > 2 or hepatic encephalopathy.
antidote: Amatoxin: NAC + silibinin + supportive (no proven antidote — supportive + chemoprotection). Gyromitra: pyridoxine + benzodiazepines. Muscarinic: atropine. Others: supportive.
redFlags: Symptom onset > 6 h post-ingestion — suspect amatoxin / gyromitra / orellanine; HIGH MORTALITY without aggressive care.
Falsely reassuring symptom-free interval (24-48 h) in amatoxin between GI and hepatic phases — anticipate hepatic injury.
Hepatic failure with INR > 2 / encephalopathy — early transplant referral.
Seizures + hepatic injury (gyromitra) — give pyridoxine.
Foraging during alcohol consumption + Coprinus = disulfiram-like reaction.
Always co-screen for paracetamol (concomitant ingestion common).

references.label: Diaz JH. Amatoxin-containing mushroom poisonings: species, toxidromes, treatments, and outcomes. Wilderness Environ Med 2018;29:111-8.
Mengs U et al. Legalon SIL: the antidote of choice in patients with acute hepatotoxicity from amatoxin poisoning. Curr Pharm Biotechnol 2012;13:1964-70.

name: Theophylline / caffeine toxicity (methylxanthines)
oneLiner: Tachycardia + tremor + vomiting + agitation; severe: ventricular arrhythmias, refractory seizures, profound hypokalaemia + hyperglycaemia + metabolic acidosis. Multi-dose activated charcoal; haemodialysis for severe.

features.mentalStatus: anxiety → agitation → seizures (often refractory)

causativeAgents: theophylline / aminophylline (oral, IV) — narrow therapeutic index (10-20 mg/L)
caffeine — massive ingestion (energy supplements, caffeine pills, pre-workout powders)
chocolate / cocoa (rare; mostly in dogs and children with very large ingestion)
management: ABC, IV access, continuous cardiac monitoring, 12-lead ECG, glucose, electrolytes (K+, Mg, phosphate), theophylline / caffeine level (q2h until peak), ABG, lactate.
MULTIPLE-DOSE ACTIVATED CHARCOAL — 50 g initially then 25 g q2h (gut dialysis effect; particularly useful for theophylline which has enterohepatic and enteroenteric circulation).
Aggressive POTASSIUM REPLACEMENT (often need K+ ≥ 40 mmol/h centrally with continuous ECG) — but anticipate rebound HYPERkalaemia after toxicity resolves (intracellular K+ redistributes).
Magnesium 2 g IV for hypomagnesaemia / arrhythmia.
Benzodiazepines first-line for seizures (often refractory — escalate to barbiturates, propofol; AVOID phenytoin in theophylline-induced seizures).
Beta-blockade for tachyarrhythmia in NON-asthmatic adults: short-acting esmolol 25-50 µg/kg/min titrated. In asthmatics use cautious low-dose β-blockade or adenosine for SVT.

HAEMODIALYSIS for severe toxicity: theophylline > 100 mg/L (acute) or > 60 mg/L (chronic, often more toxic at lower levels); seizures; arrhythmia; haemodynamic instability; cannot tolerate enteric charcoal; renal / hepatic failure. Caffeine: dialyse for severe symptoms with high level.
Vasopressors for refractory hypotension: noradrenaline (β-mediated vasodilation predominates).
Stop the offending drug; assess therapeutic level vs intentional overdose; psychiatric review if intentional.
antidote: No specific antidote. Multi-dose activated charcoal + aggressive electrolyte correction + early haemodialysis are definitive.
redFlags: Refractory seizures — escalate sedation aggressively; AVOID phenytoin.
Theophylline level > 100 mg/L acute or > 60 mg/L chronic — haemodialysis.
Chronic > acute at any given level — elderly more susceptible.
Profound hypokalaemia — replace aggressively but anticipate rebound.
Co-ingestion with caffeine + other stimulants common.

references.label: Ghannoum M et al. Extracorporeal treatment for theophylline poisoning: systematic review and recommendations from the EXTRIP workgroup. Clin Toxicol 2015;53:215-29.
Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11e — Methylxanthines.

name: Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia
oneLiner: Prolonged, RECURRENT hypoglycaemia (hours to days). Glucose alone is INSUFFICIENT — stimulates more insulin. Octreotide 50-75 µg SC q6h is the cornerstone (suppresses insulin secretion); dextrose for acute resuscitation; admit for ≥ 24 h.

features.heartRate: tachycardia (catecholamine response) or normal if β-blocked
features.mentalStatus: confusion, focal deficit (stroke mimic), seizures, coma — RECURRENT despite glucose
other: RECURRENT HYPOGLYCAEMIA — multiple episodes hours after initial resuscitation
low glucose + high C-peptide + high insulin (endogenous secretion)
elderly with renal impairment most at risk
drug interactions (sulfa antibiotics, fluoroquinolones, β-blockers) potentiate effect

causativeAgents: long-acting sulfonylureas — glibenclamide (glyburide), chlorpropamide — highest risk
shorter-acting — glipizide, gliclazide, glimepiride
meglitinides — repaglinide, nateglinide (shorter duration but same mechanism)
accidental paediatric ingestion (1 tablet can cause hypoglycaemia)
drug-drug interactions: sulfonamides, fluoroquinolones, warfarin, β-blockers
management: ABC, IV access, glucose check, continuous glucose monitoring q1h for ≥ 24 h.

ACUTE: dextrose 50% 50 mL IV bolus for hypoglycaemia (or 25% 100 mL); start D10 infusion to maintain glucose > 5.5 mmol/L. Glucagon 1 mg IM is short-acting and may deplete glycogen stores — use only as bridge.

OCTREOTIDE — somatostatin analogue, suppresses pancreatic insulin secretion. 50-75 µg SC q6h (or IV 50 µg loading + 25 µg/h infusion). FIRST-LINE in sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia. Continue for at least 24 h (longer for glibenclamide / chlorpropamide).
Activated charcoal 1 g/kg PO/NG within 1-2 h of ingestion AND airway protected.
Admit for ≥ 24 h monitoring (longer for long-acting sulfonylurea, esp. glibenclamide ~ 36-48 h).
Avoid empirical fluid restriction (dextrose infusion can cause hyponatraemia — monitor).
Identify precipitant: dose error, renal function decline, new interacting medication, intentional overdose. Pharmacy / GP review.
antidote: Octreotide — somatostatin analogue suppresses insulin release; the modern cornerstone for sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia.
redFlags: Glucose alone is INSUFFICIENT — recurrence is the rule, not the exception.
Elderly with renal impairment — extended monitoring; glibenclamide especially long-acting.
Paediatric ingestion of even 1 tablet can cause significant hypoglycaemia — admit for observation.
Stroke-mimic with focal deficit — always check glucose.
Intentional overdose — psychiatric review.

references.label: McLaughlin SA et al. Octreotide: an antidote for sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia. Ann Emerg Med 2000;36:133-8.
Glatstein M et al. Octreotide for the treatment of sulfonylurea poisoning. Clin Toxicol 2012;50:795-804.

name: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST)
oneLiner: Tinnitus + perioral numbness + metallic taste → seizures → ventricular arrhythmias / cardiac arrest after regional anaesthesia or accidental IV bolus. Intralipid 20% emulsion is the cornerstone — start IMMEDIATELY at first sign.

features.heartRate: early: hypertension + tachycardia; late: bradycardia, asystole, VT/VF
features.mentalStatus: tinnitus → perioral numbness → metallic taste → agitation → seizures → coma → cardiac arrest within minutes
other: WIDE QRS, conduction block, ventricular arrhythmia — Na-channel blockade
PROLONGED RESUSCITATION may be needed — LAST cardiac arrest can resolve over 60+ min
bupivacaine is the worst offender — most lipophilic + cardiotoxic

causativeAgents: bupivacaine, levobupivacaine, ropivacaine — most cardiotoxic
lidocaine (lignocaine), mepivacaine — less cardiotoxic but still capable
high-dose tumescent lidocaine in cosmetic surgery
regional blocks (epidural, spinal, plexus blocks) with accidental IV injection
topical absorption with extensive surface (e.g. EMLA in burns)
differentialDiagnosis: anaphylaxis to local anaesthetic preservative (rare; methylparaben)
intravascular adrenaline injection (test dose) — palpitations, transient hypertension
management: STOP injection IMMEDIATELY at first prodrome (tinnitus, perioral numbness, agitation).
ABC, 100% O₂, large-bore IV, continuous cardiac monitoring, call for help (ASRA / AAGBI protocols).

INTRALIPID 20% EMULSION (the LAST antidote): 1.5 mL/kg IV bolus over 1 min (~ 100 mL adult), then 0.25 mL/kg/min infusion. Repeat bolus q5min × 2 if no improvement. Increase infusion to 0.5 mL/kg/min if BP remains low. Maximum cumulative dose ~ 10-12 mL/kg over 30 min. Continue infusion for ≥ 10 min after haemodynamic stability.
Manage seizures with benzodiazepines (small doses to avoid further myocardial depression); AVOID propofol in cardiac arrest (myocardial depressant).

Cardiac arrest: standard ACLS BUT — REDUCE adrenaline dose to 1 µg/kg (not standard 1 mg); AVOID vasopressin, calcium channel blockers, β-blockers, lidocaine. AMIODARONE first-line for ventricular arrhythmia. PROLONG resuscitation (60+ min) — LAST arrest can resolve.
Consider cardiopulmonary bypass / ECMO early if local protocol available — bridge until LAST clears.
Manage hypotension: small adrenaline boluses + crystalloid; avoid pure α-agonist alone.
Notify operating room / consultant anaesthetist + run-in intralipid wherever the block was performed.
Audit / report — confidential incident reporting.
antidote: Intralipid 20% emulsion — proposed mechanism: lipid sink (sequesters lipophilic anaesthetic) + metabolic / cardiotonic effects. Start at first prodrome, do not wait for arrest.
redFlags: Reduce adrenaline dose 10x in LAST cardiac arrest (1 µg/kg, not 1 mg) — standard dose worsens outcome.
AVOID propofol in cardiac arrest, vasopressin, β-blockers, CCBs, lidocaine.
Prolong resuscitation — LAST arrest often resolves over 30-60 min.
Bupivacaine is most lethal — most lipophilic, longest cardiac toxicity.
Pancreatitis is a rare complication of large-volume intralipid — monitor.
ECMO availability — early activation for refractory arrest.

references.label: Neal JM et al. ASRA practice advisory on local anesthetic systemic toxicity. Reg Anesth Pain Med 2018;43:113-23.
AAGBI: Management of severe local anaesthetic toxicity (Safety Guideline) 2010.

name: Alcohol withdrawal syndrome (AWS / DTs)
oneLiner: 6-24 h after last drink: tremor + tachycardia + diaphoresis + anxiety → 24-48 h alcoholic hallucinosis / withdrawal seizures → 48-96 h delirium tremens (severe autonomic + global confusion). Long-acting benzodiazepines + CIWA-Ar guided dosing. THIAMINE BEFORE GLUCOSE.

features.mentalStatus: anxiety → tremulousness → hallucinations (visual / tactile in alcoholic hallucinosis with intact orientation) → DELIRIUM with global confusion, agitation, fluctuating consciousness in DTs
other: WITHDRAWAL SEIZURES — typically GTC, 24-48 h post-cessation; may herald DTs
DELIRIUM TREMENS — high mortality (5-15% untreated); 48-96 h post-cessation
Wernicke's encephalopathy: ophthalmoplegia + ataxia + confusion — give thiamine BEFORE glucose

causativeAgents: alcohol cessation in heavy chronic drinker (often inadvertent — admission for unrelated reason)
reduction in chronic intake (relative withdrawal)
concurrent illness, dehydration, infection, hypoglycaemia exacerbate
differentialDiagnosis: intracranial bleed / trauma (chronic alcoholics fall often)
management: ABC, IV access, continuous cardiac monitoring, glucose check, full panel: U&E, LFT, magnesium, phosphate, ABG, alcohol level, urine drug screen, infection screen, CT head if focal signs / trauma suspected.
THIAMINE 100 mg IV / 200-500 mg IV (Pabrinex 2 pairs IV TDS for ≥ 5 days if Wernicke suspected) BEFORE any glucose load — prevents precipitating Wernicke's.
Glucose for hypoglycaemia (after thiamine).
Aggressive electrolyte replacement: magnesium (often profoundly low — 2 g IV; oral supplementation continued), potassium, phosphate.
IV fluid resuscitation — patients often dehydrated.

BENZODIAZEPINES — symptom-triggered using CIWA-Ar score ≥ 8 (or 10) triggers dose: diazepam 10-20 mg IV (or PO) or lorazepam 1-4 mg IV / oxazepam 30-60 mg PO. Front-loading (large doses in first hours) reduces cumulative dose. Long-acting diazepam preferred in normal hepatic function; lorazepam / oxazepam if cirrhosis (no active metabolites).
Refractory DTs — escalate to phenobarbital IV (200-260 mg loading then titrated), dexmedetomidine infusion adjunct, ICU + propofol / midazolam infusion if intubated.
Seizure management: benzodiazepines (acute); reassess for other causes if focal or unresponsive.
Address underlying alcohol use disorder: motivational interviewing, refer to addiction services, naltrexone / acamprosate / disulfiram options for maintenance.
Avoid antipsychotics as primary therapy (lower seizure threshold) — adjunct only for persistent agitation.
antidote: No specific antidote. Benzodiazepines + thiamine + electrolyte replacement + supportive care.
redFlags: Wernicke's encephalopathy (ophthalmoplegia + ataxia + confusion) — high-dose IV thiamine.
Withdrawal seizures — herald DTs; escalate prophylaxis.
DTs — high mortality untreated; ICU.
Co-existing infection / trauma / metabolic derangement — search aggressively.
Hepatic failure with encephalopathy — prefer lorazepam / oxazepam (no active metabolites).
Concomitant benzodiazepine / opioid use disorder — multi-drug withdrawal more complex.
Pregnancy + AWS — same management; benzodiazepines preferable to seizures / DTs.

references.label: Mayo-Smith MF et al. Management of alcohol withdrawal delirium: an evidence-based practice guideline. Arch Intern Med 2004;164:1405-12.
NICE CG100: Alcohol-use disorders: diagnosis and clinical management of alcohol-related physical complications. 2010 (updated).

name: Opioid withdrawal syndrome
oneLiner: Distinct from intoxication: mydriasis + lacrimation + rhinorrhoea + piloerection + yawning + GI cramps + diarrhoea + dysphoria. Rarely life-threatening but very distressing. Buprenorphine induction (use COWS) is modern best practice.

features.skin: PILOERECTION (gooseflesh), diaphoresis, lacrimation, rhinorrhoea — autonomic features
features.mentalStatus: anxious, dysphoric, restless, drug-seeking; mentation intact
features.bowelSounds: hyperactive — abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea
other: neonatal abstinence syndrome in newborns of opioid-using mothers (irritability, high-pitched cry, poor feeding)

causativeAgents: cessation of long-term opioid use (heroin, prescription opioids, methadone, buprenorphine)
naloxone reversal in dependent users (rapid-onset)
rotation between opioids without adequate equianalgesic conversion
neonatal abstinence — maternal opioid use during pregnancy
management: Assess severity with COWS (Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale): 5-12 mild, 13-24 moderate, 25-36 moderately severe, > 36 severe.

BUPRENORPHINE INDUCTION — modern best practice for moderate-severe withdrawal: 4-8 mg sublingual once COWS ≥ 12 (precipitates withdrawal if given too early — at least 8-12 h since last short-acting opioid, 24-48 h since methadone). Titrate 4-8 mg q1-2h to total 16-24 mg day 1, then maintain.
METHADONE alternative: 20-40 mg PO once-daily; titrate over days; only in specialist settings.

Symptomatic adjuncts: clonidine 0.1-0.2 mg PO q4-6h (autonomic features); ondansetron / metoclopramide for nausea; loperamide for diarrhoea; NSAIDs / paracetamol for myalgia; benzodiazepines short-term for anxiety / insomnia (with caution given misuse potential).
IV fluids if dehydrated from vomiting / diarrhoea.
Connect with addiction services / opioid agonist therapy programme — buprenorphine induction in the ED is an evidence-based gateway to long-term treatment.
Naloxone reversal in dependent user — short-acting; manage symptomatically until naloxone wears off; do not give additional opioid solely to relieve withdrawal in the acute reversal phase.
Neonatal abstinence: scoring (Finnegan), morphine titration, supportive nursing care (low-stimulation environment); methadone or buprenorphine alternatives.
antidote: No specific antidote. Buprenorphine induction is the modern best practice — directly treats withdrawal while initiating maintenance.
redFlags: Suicidal ideation during withdrawal — risk of relapse + overdose; psychiatric review.
Pregnancy + opioid withdrawal — preferred treatment is methadone or buprenorphine maintenance (NOT detox during pregnancy; risk of fetal distress / loss).
Concomitant alcohol / benzodiazepine withdrawal — multi-drug withdrawal more complex; alcohol withdrawal is the lethality concern.
Recently reversed with naloxone — anticipate re-sedation as naloxone wears off; do not discharge prematurely.
Polysubstance use, fentanyl analogues / nitazenes — incomplete reversal common.

references.label: WHO Guidelines for the Identification and Management of Substance Use and Substance Use Disorders in Pregnancy. 2014.
ASAM National Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Opioid Use Disorder. 2020 focused update.

name: Inhalant abuse (volatile solvents / huffing / sudden sniffing death)
oneLiner: Euphoria + dizziness + confusion after huffing solvents / aerosols; risk of SUDDEN SNIFFING DEATH from catecholamine-sensitised cardiac arrhythmia. Avoid catecholamines; use β-blocker for arrhythmia.

features.skin: perioral / nasal dermatitis ('huffer's rash') — distinctive; solvent smell on breath / clothing
features.mentalStatus: euphoria → ataxia → confusion → coma
other: SUDDEN SNIFFING DEATH SYNDROME — catecholamine-sensitised myocardium + halogenated hydrocarbon → VF on startle / exertion
chronic abuse: peripheral neuropathy (n-hexane), encephalopathy (toluene), hepatorenal toxicity (chlorinated hydrocarbons), bone marrow suppression (benzene)

causativeAgents: halogenated hydrocarbons: 1,1-difluoroethane (computer duster, refrigerants), tetrafluoroethane — SUDDEN DEATH RISK
aromatic hydrocarbons: toluene (glue, paint thinner), benzene, xylene
aliphatic: n-hexane (rubber cement, contact glue) — peripheral neuropathy
ketones: acetone (nail polish remover)
nitrites: amyl / butyl / isobutyl ('poppers') — methaemoglobinaemia + vasodilation
nitrous oxide ('nos', whippets) — B12 inactivation, neurologic deficit with chronic use
petrol / gasoline (intentional sniffing — neurologic damage)
management: ABC, IV access, continuous cardiac monitoring, 12-lead ECG, glucose check.
REMOVE FROM EXPOSURE; avoid startling or stressing the patient (catecholamine-induced VF risk).
100% O₂ if hypoxic.

CARDIAC ARRHYTHMIA: β-BLOCKER (esmolol 25-50 µg/kg/min, propranolol 0.5-1 mg IV) — counters catecholamine sensitivity. AVOID adrenaline / catecholamines if possible (worsens VF risk). Lidocaine, amiodarone for VT/VF arrest per ACLS.
Methaemoglobinaemia (nitrite use): methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg IV.
Treat seizures with benzodiazepines.
Supportive care; observation typically 4-6 h post-exposure if asymptomatic.
Substance use counselling, often involving family / school in adolescents.
Identify and remediate environmental access (locked storage of solvents).
antidote: No specific antidote (except methylene blue for nitrite-induced methaemoglobinaemia). Avoid catecholamines; β-blocker for arrhythmia.
redFlags: Sudden cardiac arrest in adolescent — consider inhalant; β-blocker, avoid extra catecholamines.
