Nitrite use + cyanosis unresponsive to O₂ — methaemoglobinaemia; methylene blue.
Chronic toluene abuse + metabolic acidosis + hypokalaemia + RTA — distinctive.
Nitrous oxide chronic + neurologic deficit (myelopathy, subacute combined degeneration) — B12 deficiency-like; vitamin B12 replacement, cessation.
Perioral 'huffer's rash' + glue smell — pathognomonic.

references.label: Bowen SE. Two serious and challenging medical complications associated with volatile substance misuse: sudden sniffing death and fetal solvent syndrome. Subst Use Misuse 2011;46(Suppl 1):68-72.
Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11e — Inhalants.

name: GHB / GBL overdose
oneLiner: Coma → ABRUPT AWAKENING 1-4 h later (the 'club drug coma'). Bradycardia, hypothermia, respiratory depression. Naloxone / flumazenil ineffective. Pure supportive care; avoid intubation if airway protected and awakening expected.

features.mentalStatus: rapid-onset coma (15-30 min after dose) → ABRUPT AWAKENING 1-4 h later, often combative or confused on emergence
other: MYOCLONIC JERKS / seizure-like activity during coma — not true seizure

causativeAgents: gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB) — date-rape drug, recreational, narcolepsy treatment (sodium oxybate)
gamma-butyrolactone (GBL) — solvent / industrial precursor; metabolised to GHB in vivo
1,4-butanediol (1,4-BD) — also converts to GHB
differentialDiagnosis: opioid overdose (also coma + bradypnoea; but naloxone-responsive)
management: ABC, IV access, continuous cardiac monitoring, glucose check.
Supportive care — bag-mask ventilation if hypoventilating; positioning (lateral / left lateral decubitus).
Naloxone / flumazenil are NOT effective — do not waste time waiting for response.
Activated charcoal NOT useful (rapid absorption, low yield).

Avoid intubation if possible — patients typically awaken abruptly 1-4 h post-ingestion. Intubate only for: aspiration, refractory hypoxia / inadequate ventilation, prolonged coma beyond expected window. Use minimal sedation pre-intubation (rapid awakening may risk extubation injury).
Cooling reversal: passive rewarming for mild hypothermia.
Manage bradycardia: atropine 0.5 mg IV if symptomatic / hypotensive; rarely needed.
Anticipate combative awakening — soft restraints, environment protection, brief sedation IF necessary (small doses; agitation usually self-resolves over minutes).
Withdrawal syndrome in chronic users (severe, similar to alcohol DTs) — admit for benzodiazepine titration.
antidote: No specific antidote. Naloxone and flumazenil are NOT effective. Supportive care is the cornerstone.
redFlags: Co-ingestion with alcohol / MDMA / methamphetamine — additive respiratory depression / cardiotoxicity.
Date-rape suspicion — chain of evidence; consider forensic / safeguarding referral (GHB has short detection window in blood and urine — collect early).
Chronic user withdrawal — severe, similar to DTs; admit, benzodiazepines + baclofen + phenobarbital.
Aspiration — beware silent aspiration in coma.
Combative emergence — anticipate, plan for environment safety.

references.label: Liechti ME et al. Pharmacology and toxicology of gamma-hydroxybutyrate. CNS Drug Rev 2006.
Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11e — γ-Hydroxybutyric Acid.

name: Datura / plant-based anticholinergic poisoning
oneLiner: Adolescent or unintentional ingestion of Datura / jimsonweed / Brugmansia: severe anticholinergic toxidrome — hours of agitated delirium with mydriasis, dry skin, hyperthermia, urinary retention. Benzodiazepines first-line; physostigmine if pure delirium + normal ECG.

features.pupils: MARKEDLY DILATED, sluggish — often persists 24-48 h
features.mentalStatus: agitated delirium, picking behaviour, vivid hallucinations (lilliputian visual common), often dramatic for hours
other: PROLONGED COURSE — symptoms can last 24-72 h (longer than typical pharmaceutical anticholinergic) because plant alkaloids absorb slowly + persist
seeds ('thorn-apple') and tea preparations common in adolescent recreational use

causativeAgents: Datura stramonium (jimsonweed, thorn apple) — seeds, leaves, tea
Atropa belladonna (deadly nightshade)
Brugmansia (angel's trumpet) — flowers, leaves
Hyoscyamus niger (henbane)
Mandragora officinarum (mandrake)
differentialDiagnosis: pharmaceutical anticholinergic (TCAs, antihistamines, antipsychotics) — usually shorter course
psychosis / acute confusion of other cause
management: ABC, IV access, continuous cardiac monitoring, 12-lead ECG (rule out TCA co-ingestion / Na-channel features), glucose, full panel.
Cooling: undress, evaporative cooling; target core temp < 38.5°C.
IV fluid resuscitation — rhabdomyolysis risk.
BENZODIAZEPINES first-line for agitation (lorazepam 2-4 mg IV titrated; diazepam alternative). Avoid antipsychotics (worsen anticholinergic load, lower seizure threshold).
FOLEY catheter for urinary retention if present.
Activated charcoal 1 g/kg PO/NG within 1-2 h AND airway protected; multiple-dose may be considered if seeds (slow release).

Physostigmine 1-2 mg IV slowly (over 5 min) for pure anticholinergic delirium WITHOUT TCA features and with normal ECG (no QRS widening, no conduction delay). Discuss with toxicology first. Often dramatically effective ("Antagonising the anticholinergic" effect — but can precipitate seizures or bradyarrhythmia if used in TCA poisoning).
Prolonged observation — symptoms can last 24-72 h.
Adolescent psychosocial review — recreational ingestion often signals concerning patterns; addiction / psychology referral.
antidote: Physostigmine — reverses central + peripheral anticholinergic effects; reserved for pure plant anticholinergic delirium with normal ECG. Benzodiazepines are the mainstay for agitation.
redFlags: Co-ingested TCA or other Na-channel blocker — DO NOT give physostigmine.
Core temp > 40°C — aggressive cooling.
Rhabdomyolysis (dark urine, rising CK) — IV fluids.
Seizures — benzodiazepines.
Prolonged course — admit; arrange home reassessment / psychiatric follow-up.
Adolescent recreational use — common cluster outbreaks (Datura tea recipes circulating); public health implications.

references.label: Wiebe TH et al. Datura stramonium intoxication: a clinical and pharmacological review. Clin Toxicol 2008.
Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11e — Anticholinergics.

name: Synthetic cannabinoid / synthetic cathinone (bath salts) intoxication
oneLiner: Atypical sympathomimetic — extreme agitation, paranoid psychosis, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY (cathinones especially), seizures. Urine drug screen negative for cannabis / amphetamine. Benzodiazepines + cooling + supportive.

features.mentalStatus: extreme agitation, paranoia, psychosis, hallucinations, violent behaviour
other: RHABDOMYOLYSIS with renal failure — particularly cathinones ("bath salts") and synthetic cannabinoids (Spice / K2)
seizures more common than with classical cannabis / amphetamines
MDPV (cathinone) often causes prolonged psychosis / re-presentation cycles
urine drug screen typically negative — laboratory diagnosis difficult

causativeAgents: synthetic cannabinoids: 'Spice', 'K2', 'Black Mamba', AB-FUBINACA, MDMB-CHMICA, ADB-PINACA — potent CB1 receptor full agonists (vs partial agonist THC)
synthetic cathinones: 'bath salts', MDPV (methylenedioxypyrovalerone), mephedrone (4-MMC), methylone, α-PVP ('flakka')
Other NPS (novel psychoactive substances): 2C-B, 25I-NBOMe, etc.
management: ABC, IV access, continuous cardiac monitoring, 12-lead ECG, glucose check, full panel: CK, U&E (AKI), urinalysis (myoglobinuria), troponin, lactate, ABG.

Aggressive BENZODIAZEPINES (lorazepam 2-4 mg IV q5min, or diazepam 5-10 mg IV) — first-line for agitation, hypertension, tachycardia, seizures. Cumulative doses often very large (50-100 mg lorazepam equivalents).
Active cooling: undress, evaporative cooling, cool IV fluids; aggressive target temp < 38.5°C within 30 min.
Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation for rhabdomyolysis prevention (target urine output > 1-2 mL/kg/h).
Hypertension: titrate benzodiazepines first; vasodilators (nicardipine, phentolamine) if persistent.
AVOID antipsychotics as primary (lower seizure threshold; worsen hyperthermia via dopamine block) — use only as adjunct after high-dose benzodiazepines if needed.
Severe / refractory: intubation + non-depolarising paralysis + cooling + ICU.
Renal support: monitor for AKI; renal replacement therapy if needed.
Psychiatric input — psychosis may persist 24-72 h after metabolic clearance.
Public health / surveillance — outbreak clusters common, alerting needed.
antidote: No specific antidote. Aggressive benzodiazepines + cooling + IV fluids + renal support.
redFlags: Core temp > 41°C — aggressive cooling + paralysis.
Rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuric AKI — IV fluids, renal replacement.
Seizures, refractory psychosis — high-dose benzodiazepines, propofol / barbiturate escalation.
Drug screen typically NEGATIVE — clinical diagnosis; do not be falsely reassured.
Cluster presentations — outbreak from contaminated batch; alert public health.
Prolonged psychosis — psychiatric admission; reassess capacity.

references.label: Spaderna M et al. Spicing things up: synthetic cannabinoids. Psychopharmacology 2013;228:525-40.
Prosser JM, Nelson LS. The toxicology of bath salts: a review of synthetic cathinones. J Med Toxicol 2012;8:33-42.

name: Malignant hyperthermia (MH) — anaesthesia trigger
oneLiner: Hypermetabolic crisis in the operating theatre: rising end-tidal CO₂ + masseter spasm + tachycardia + hyperthermia + acidosis after volatile anaesthetic or succinylcholine. DANTROLENE 2.5 mg/kg IV immediately, repeat to 10 mg/kg total. STOP trigger, switch to non-triggering agent.

features.respiratoryRate: tachypnoea if spontaneously breathing; RISING END-TIDAL CO₂ (the earliest specific sign) if mechanically ventilated
features.temperature: HYPERTHERMIA (LATE sign; rises 1-2°C every 5 min in severe) — may exceed 42-44°C
features.skin: diaphoretic, mottled cyanosis as O₂ extraction overwhelmed
features.mentalStatus: anaesthetised — diagnosed by physiology
other: MASSETER SPASM after succinylcholine — early clue
HYPERCARBIA out of proportion to ventilation — KEY early sign
muscle rigidity, dark cola urine (myoglobinuria), DIC late

causativeAgents: VOLATILE ANAESTHETICS: halothane (highest risk), isoflurane, sevoflurane, desflurane, enflurane
SUCCINYLCHOLINE (suxamethonium) — depolarising neuromuscular blocker
GENETIC SUSCEPTIBILITY: ryanodine receptor (RYR1) and CACNA1S mutations — autosomal dominant
Associated myopathies: Central Core Disease, King-Denborough syndrome
differentialDiagnosis: inadequate anaesthesia (light anaesthesia + pain → catecholamine response)
neuroleptic malignant syndrome (in PACU, post-antipsychotic exposure)
management: CALL FOR HELP — open the MH kit / activate MH protocol immediately.
STOP volatile anaesthetic + succinylcholine; switch to non-triggering total IV anaesthesia (propofol, opioid, non-depolarising muscle relaxant).
HYPERVENTILATE with 100% O₂ at high flows (10 L/min); change soda lime / circuit if practical (delays response otherwise).

DANTROLENE 2.5 mg/kg IV BOLUS — reconstitute as quickly as possible (new ryanodex formulation faster than older dantrium); repeat 1 mg/kg q5-10min until physiology normalises (cumulative dose may exceed 10 mg/kg). Continue 1 mg/kg q6h for ≥ 24 h to prevent recurrence.
Active cooling: ice packs to groin / axillae, cold IV fluids, gastric / bladder lavage with cold saline; aim for core temp < 38.5°C. STOP cooling at 38°C to avoid overshoot.
Manage hyperkalaemia: calcium chloride 10% 10 mL IV, insulin-dextrose, sodium bicarbonate (acidosis + K), hyperventilation; haemodialysis if refractory.
Manage arrhythmias: standard ACLS; AVOID calcium channel blockers (dantrolene + verapamil → severe hyperkalaemia + myocardial depression).
Aggressive IV fluid + diuresis (mannitol / furosemide) to protect renal function from myoglobinuric AKI.
Coagulopathy / DIC — FFP, cryoprecipitate, platelets as indicated.
Admit to ICU for ≥ 24 h post-event; recurrence is described.
Counsel patient + family — refer for MH genetic testing / caffeine-halothane contracture test; alert MHAUS / national registry; provide MH-safe anaesthesia plan for future surgery.
antidote: Dantrolene — inhibits ryanodine receptor calcium release; the only specific antidote. New ryanodex formulation reconstitutes much faster than older dantrium.
redFlags: Rising ETCO₂ early — diagnose BEFORE temperature rises (temperature is a LATE sign).
Masseter spasm + tachycardia after succinylcholine — possible MH; switch to TIVA.
AVOID calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem) + dantrolene — severe hyperkalaemia + myocardial depression.
Recurrence in 24 h — continue dantrolene prophylaxis 1 mg/kg q6h.
Hyperkalaemia with arrhythmia — calcium, insulin-dextrose, hyperventilation.
Genetic counselling for patient + first-degree relatives — autosomal dominant inheritance.
MHAUS / national MH hotline available 24/7 — call for guidance during a crisis.

references.label: Glahn KP et al. Recognizing and managing a malignant hyperthermia crisis: guidelines from the European MH Group. Br J Anaesth 2010;105:417-20.
MHAUS — Malignant Hyperthermia Association of the United States (www.mhaus.org), hotline +1-800-MH-HYPER.

name: Strychnine poisoning
oneLiner: AWAKE patient with painful generalised muscle spasms / opisthotonos / risus sardonicus triggered by stimuli, between attacks completely lucid (distinguishes from seizure / tetanus). Aggressive benzodiazepines + paralysis + ventilation; cooling.

features.respiratoryRate: tachypnoea early; respiratory arrest from chest-wall spasm late
features.mentalStatus: LUCID between spasms — KEY differentiator from seizure (post-ictal confusion absent)
other: RISUS SARDONICUS, OPISTHOTONOS, generalised painful spasms triggered by minor stimuli (light, sound, touch)
high anion gap metabolic / lactic acidosis

causativeAgents: strychnine — rodenticide (largely phased out but persists in some countries / illegal use)
contaminated street drugs (rare adulterant)
Strychnos seeds (nux vomica) — traditional medicine
differentialDiagnosis: tetanus (also rigidity + spasms, but trismus + slower onset days-weeks, no spasm-free intervals)
management: QUIET, DARK environment — minimise stimuli that trigger spasms.
ABC; early intubation + non-depolarising paralysis + mechanical ventilation for severe / repeated spasms (prevents chest-wall paralysis suffocation).
Aggressive BENZODIAZEPINES (diazepam 5-10 mg IV q5min, lorazepam 2-4 mg IV) — first-line for spasms, hypertension, tachycardia.
BARBITURATES (thiopental, phenobarbital) for refractory cases.
Active cooling for hyperthermia.
Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation for rhabdomyolysis prevention; monitor CK, U&E, K+, urinalysis (myoglobinuria); consider haemodialysis if AKI.
Activated charcoal 1 g/kg PO/NG if recent ingestion AND airway protected (often intubated).
Avoid succinylcholine (depolarisation may exacerbate spasm + hyperkalaemia risk from rhabdomyolysis); use non-depolarising agents.
Monitor for hyperthermia overshoot during paralysis; ETCO₂ during ventilation.
Symptoms self-limit within 24-72 h as drug cleared; supportive care during that window is curative.
antidote: No specific antidote. Aggressive benzodiazepine / barbiturate sedation + paralysis + ventilation + cooling are the cornerstones.
redFlags: AWAKE between spasms — distinguishes from seizure / NMS.
Chest-wall spasm + respiratory failure — early intubation + paralysis lifesaving.
Rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuric AKI — IV fluids, renal replacement if needed.
Avoid succinylcholine — use non-depolarising paralytic.
Quiet, dark environment essential — light / noise triggers spasms.
Hyperthermia overshoot during paralysis — monitor core temperature.

references.label: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11e — Strychnine.
Wood DM et al. Case report: survival after deliberate strychnine self-poisoning. Crit Care 2002;6:456-9.

name: NSAID overdose
oneLiner: Most NSAID overdoses are benign (nausea, abdominal pain). Severe ingestion: AKI, seizures (mefenamic acid + bupropion-class), metabolic acidosis, GI haemorrhage. Supportive care; activated charcoal early; no specific antidote.

features.mentalStatus: normal usually; seizures with mefenamic acid; coma with massive ibuprofen
features.bowelSounds: hyperactive with abdominal pain; haematemesis / melaena if GI bleed
other: ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY — prostaglandin-dependent renal blood flow
metabolic acidosis — high anion gap in massive ibuprofen ingestion
SEIZURES — mefenamic acid the classical offender, often within 4-6 h of ingestion

causativeAgents: ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac (common over-the-counter)
mefenamic acid — distinctive seizure risk
indomethacin, ketorolac, etoricoxib, celecoxib
aspirin (high-dose) — treat as salicylate toxidrome (see salicylate-toxidrome record)
management: ABC, IV access, continuous cardiac monitoring, glucose check, full panel: U&E, ABG, lactate, FBC, INR, salicylate AND paracetamol levels (always co-screen), ECG.
Activated charcoal 1 g/kg PO/NG if within 1-2 h AND airway protected.
IV fluid resuscitation — most patients dehydrated; renal protection.
PPI / H2-blocker for GI symptoms / haemorrhage; endoscopy if upper GI bleed.
Manage AKI: stop NSAID, IV fluids, monitor U&E + urine output; renal replacement therapy if severe.
Seizures (mefenamic acid): benzodiazepines first-line.
Metabolic acidosis: IV fluid; consider bicarbonate for severe pH < 7.2.
Haemodialysis is occasionally useful for refractory acidosis / AKI / severe massive ibuprofen ingestion (highly protein-bound — efficacy limited).
Supportive care — most overdoses resolve within 24 h with simple measures.
Psychiatric review if intentional.
antidote: No specific antidote. Supportive care; activated charcoal early; renal protection.
redFlags: Mefenamic acid + seizures — early benzodiazepines; admit for ≥ 12 h observation.
Massive ibuprofen ingestion (> 400 mg/kg) with metabolic acidosis / coma / AKI — ICU consideration.
Co-ingestion (paracetamol especially) — always co-screen.
Elderly / volume-depleted / pre-existing CKD — disproportionate AKI risk.
GI haemorrhage — endoscopy.
Pregnancy — premature closure of ductus arteriosus from late-T3 NSAID use; obstetric input.

references.label: Hall AH et al. Ibuprofen overdose: 126 cases. Ann Emerg Med 1986;15:1308-13.
Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11e — Nonsteroidal Anti-inflammatory Drugs.

name: Isoniazid (INH) toxicity
oneLiner: Classic triad: refractory seizures + metabolic (lactic) acidosis + coma after INH overdose. Pyridoxine is the antidote — give gram-for-gram with the ingested INH (or 70 mg/kg, max 5 g, if dose unknown).

features.bloodPressure: normal or hypotension in severe cases
features.temperature: normothermia or hyperthermia with status epilepticus
features.mentalStatus: agitation → seizures (often status, anticonvulsant-refractory) → coma
other: seizures typically within 30-120 min of large ingestion

causativeAgents: isoniazid (anti-tuberculous therapy) — acute overdose, often intentional
co-ingestion with other anti-TB drugs (rifampicin, pyrazinamide)
differentialDiagnosis: other causes of status epilepticus (other toxins, structural, metabolic)
management: ABC; protect airway; IV access; continuous monitoring; check glucose, lactate, blood gas.
Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) IV: 1 g pyridoxine per 1 g isoniazid ingested if the dose is known; if unknown, 70 mg/kg up to a maximum of 5 g IV. Repeat if seizures recur.
Benzodiazepines (e.g. diazepam / lorazepam) for seizures — synergistic with pyridoxine; INH seizures are often refractory to anticonvulsants without pyridoxine.
Treat metabolic acidosis — usually resolves once seizures controlled; sodium bicarbonate if severe.
Activated charcoal 1 g/kg if early presentation AND airway protected.
Haemodialysis is rarely needed but can remove INH in massive ingestion with renal impairment.
antidote: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) IV — gram-for-gram with ingested INH, or 70 mg/kg (max 5 g) if dose unknown. Replenishes GABA synthesis to terminate seizures.
redFlags: Status epilepticus refractory to benzodiazepines — give/repeat pyridoxine immediately.
Severe high-anion-gap (lactic) acidosis.
Coma / airway compromise — intubate.
Massive ingestion with renal impairment — consider haemodialysis.

references.label: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11e — Antituberculous Medications (isoniazid).
Morrow LE et al. Pyridoxine for isoniazid-induced seizures — poison centre experience. Am J Emerg Med 2018.

name: Methaemoglobinaemia
oneLiner: Cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen + 'chocolate-brown' blood + saturation gap (SpO₂ ~ 85% that won't rise). Methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg IV slowly — but withhold/seek alternative in G6PD deficiency.

features.skin: central cyanosis (slate-grey) that does NOT improve with supplemental oxygen
features.mentalStatus: headache, fatigue → confusion, coma at high methaemoglobin levels
other: normal PaO₂ on blood gas despite cyanosis
symptoms broadly correlate with MetHb %: > 20% symptomatic, > 50% severe, > 70% potentially fatal

causativeAgents: oxidising drugs: dapsone, local anaesthetics (benzocaine, prilocaine, lidocaine), nitrates/nitrites, sulfonamides, metoclopramide, primaquine
rasburicase (contraindicated in G6PD deficiency)
aniline dyes, nitrobenzene, naphthalene
amyl/sodium nitrite (including cyanide-kit use)
differentialDiagnosis: hypoxaemic respiratory failure (but PaO₂ normal here)
cyanide toxicity (also cyanosis with normal PaO₂)
management: High-flow oxygen; remove the offending agent; IV access; co-oximetry to measure methaemoglobin (standard pulse oximetry is unreliable).
Methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg IV over ~ 5 min for symptomatic methaemoglobinaemia (commonly MetHb > 20-30%, or lower if symptomatic/comorbid); may repeat after 30-60 min if needed.

If G6PD deficiency known or suspected: methylene blue is relatively contraindicated (ineffective and risks haemolysis) — use ascorbic acid (vitamin C), and consider exchange transfusion / hyperbaric oxygen for severe cases.
Avoid more than ~ 2 doses of methylene blue (paradoxical methaemoglobinaemia and haemolysis at high cumulative dose).
Supportive care; treat the specific causative toxin (e.g. dapsone — see dapsone toxicity).
antidote: Methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg IV slowly (acts via NADPH-dependent reduction of methaemoglobin). Ascorbic acid is the alternative when methylene blue is contraindicated (e.g. G6PD deficiency).
redFlags: Methaemoglobin > 30% or symptomatic — give methylene blue.
G6PD deficiency — methylene blue ineffective/harmful; use ascorbic acid / exchange transfusion.
Persistent or recurrent methaemoglobinaemia (long-acting agents e.g. dapsone) — anticipate repeat dosing.
Failure to respond to methylene blue — reconsider G6PD deficiency, sulfhaemoglobinaemia, or ongoing absorption.

references.label: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11e — Methemoglobin Inducers.
Cortazzo JA, Lichtman AD. Methemoglobinemia: a review and recommendations for management. J Cardiothorac Vasc Anesth 2014.

name: Valproic acid (sodium valproate) toxicity
oneLiner: CNS depression + hyperammonaemia (even with normal LFTs) ± metabolic acidosis after VPA overdose. Supportive care; L-carnitine for hyperammonaemic encephalopathy / hepatotoxicity; haemodialysis for massive/severe poisoning.

features.mentalStatus: drowsiness → coma; hyperammonaemic encephalopathy (confusion, asterixis) even without hepatic failure

causativeAgents: sodium valproate / valproic acid / divalproex — acute overdose
chronic supratherapeutic dosing (hyperammonaemia can occur at therapeutic levels too)
differentialDiagnosis: other causes of high anion-gap acidosis
management: ABC; protect airway in coma; IV access; monitor; serial VPA levels, ammonia, LFTs, lactate, blood gas, electrolytes, FBC.
Activated charcoal 1 g/kg if early ingestion AND airway protected; multi-dose charcoal may be considered for large enteric-coated/extended-release ingestions.

L-carnitine (levocarnitine) for hyperammonaemic encephalopathy, hepatotoxicity, or significant VPA toxicity: a reported regimen is 100 mg/kg IV (max ~ 6 g) loading, then 50 mg/kg (max 3 g) IV every 8 h until clinical improvement and falling ammonia. Optimal dose/route not firmly established.
Haemodialysis for severe poisoning (e.g. very high VPA levels, coma, refractory acidosis, shock, hyperammonaemia not responding) — VPA is dialysable at toxic levels (saturated protein binding).
Supportive care: correct electrolytes, support blood pressure, manage cerebral oedema.
antidote: L-carnitine (levocarnitine) IV for valproate-induced hyperammonaemia / hepatotoxicity — replenishes carnitine to restore the urea cycle and fatty-acid oxidation. Not a complete antidote; supportive care and dialysis remain key.
redFlags: Coma / airway compromise.
Hyperammonaemic encephalopathy — give L-carnitine.
Very high VPA level, refractory acidosis, shock, cerebral oedema — urgent haemodialysis.
Hepatotoxicity or bone-marrow suppression.

references.label: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11e — Valproic Acid.
Perrott J et al. L-carnitine for acute valproic acid overdose: a systematic review of published cases. Ann Pharmacother 2010.

name: Superwarfarin (long-acting anticoagulant rodenticide) poisoning
oneLiner: Brodifacoum and other 'superwarfarins' cause profound, PROLONGED coagulopathy (weeks to months). Treat bleeding with vitamin K1 + factors; expect to need very high-dose oral vitamin K1 for weeks-to-months, guided by INR.

features.mentalStatus: normal unless intracranial haemorrhage
other: markedly prolonged INR/PT (factors II, VII, IX, X)
brodifacoum half-life up to 20-30 days → coagulopathy persists for weeks to months

causativeAgents: brodifacoum, difenacoum, bromadiolone, difethialone (second-generation anticoagulant rodenticides)
intentional ingestion, contaminated illicit drugs (synthetic cannabinoid outbreaks), accidental paediatric ingestion
management: ABC; IV access; check INR/PT, aPTT, FBC; type and screen if bleeding.
Active bleeding: 4-factor PCC and/or fresh frozen plasma for immediate factor replacement, PLUS vitamin K1 (phytomenadione) IV.
No bleeding but elevated INR: high-dose oral vitamin K1; a single paediatric ingestion of a small amount often does not require treatment — observe and check INR at 48-72 h.

Confirmed superwarfarin poisoning needs PROLONGED high-dose oral vitamin K1 — reported maintenance requirements average ~ 60 mg/day (range 15-600 mg/day), titrated to INR, sometimes for 3 months or more.
Serial INR monitoring (after vitamin K1 stopped, recheck to detect rebound); brodifacoum serum levels guide duration if available.
Do NOT give vitamin K1 prophylactically before INR rises in an asymptomatic single ingestion — it masks the diagnostic INR; follow INR instead.
antidote: Vitamin K1 (phytomenadione) — high dose and PROLONGED (weeks to months), titrated to INR. PCC/FFP for active bleeding.
redFlags: Intracranial or other major haemorrhage — PCC/FFP + IV vitamin K1, urgent.
Stopping vitamin K1 too early — coagulopathy rebounds for weeks; taper guided by INR.
Very large oral vitamin K1 doses (tens of tablets/day) — adherence is a major challenge.
Intentional/contaminated exposures — consider co-ingestants and toxicology/haematology referral.

references.label: King N, Tran MH. Long-acting anticoagulant rodenticide (superwarfarin) poisoning: pathophysiology to laboratory-guided clinical management. Transfus Med Rev 2015.
Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11e — Antithrombotics / rodenticides.

name: Hydrofluoric acid (HF) exposure
oneLiner: Severe, often delayed pain out of proportion to a deceptively minor-looking burn; fluoride chelates calcium/magnesium → life-threatening hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hyperkalaemia and arrhythmia. Calcium is the antidote (topical gel, then SC/IV/intra-arterial).

features.skin: burn may look minor initially; severe deep pain; whitening/blistering develops; pain out of proportion to appearance
features.mentalStatus: anxiety, then obtundation if profound electrolyte derangement

causativeAgents: industrial and domestic hydrofluoric acid (glass etching, rust removers, semiconductor cleaning, wheel cleaners)
ammonium bifluoride and related fluoride compounds
differentialDiagnosis: other acid/chemical burns (less delayed pain, less systemic Ca derangement)
management: Staff PPE; remove contaminated clothing; copious irrigation of skin with water for ≥ 15-30 min.
Topical calcium gluconate gel (e.g. 2.5% — prepared by mixing calcium gluconate into a water-soluble lubricant) massaged into dermal exposures.

Persistent pain despite topical: intradermal/subcutaneous calcium gluconate infiltration (10% calcium gluconate, NOT calcium chloride — chloride causes tissue necrosis); intra-arterial or Bier-block calcium gluconate for digital/hand burns refractory to topical.
Systemic / large-area / ingestion / inhalation exposure: IV calcium gluconate and IV magnesium; correct potassium; treat hypocalcaemia even empirically in high-risk exposures before levels return.
Continuous ECG monitoring; monitor ionised calcium, magnesium, potassium frequently; treat arrhythmias.
Large surface-area (> ~ 1% BSA concentrated, or any systemic features) — admit to ICU; haemodialysis can help refractory hypocalcaemia / fluoride load.
antidote: Calcium (gluconate) — topical gel first, then SC infiltration, intra-arterial / IV for systemic toxicity. Magnesium and potassium correction as needed.
redFlags: Concentrated HF or large body-surface-area exposure — anticipate fatal hypocalcaemia/arrhythmia.
Severe pain despite normal-looking skin — do not under-treat.
Hypocalcaemia / prolonged QT / hyperkalaemia on ECG — IV calcium, ICU.
Inhalation — airway oedema and pulmonary toxicity; ingestion — corrosive plus systemic fluoride.

references.label: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11e — Hydrofluoric Acid and Fluorides.
McKee D et al. A review of hydrofluoric acid burn management. Plast Surg (Oakv) 2014.

name: Dapsone toxicity
oneLiner: Methaemoglobinaemia + haemolytic anaemia from a very long-acting oxidant (half-life prolonged by enterohepatic recycling). Methylene blue for methaemoglobinaemia + multi-dose activated charcoal to shorten the half-life.

features.skin: cyanosis (methaemoglobinaemia) unresponsive to oxygen; pallor/jaundice from haemolysis
features.mentalStatus: headache, lethargy → confusion in severe methaemoglobinaemia
other: recurrent/prolonged methaemoglobinaemia (dapsone half-life up to ~ 80 h with enterohepatic recirculation)

causativeAgents: dapsone (leprosy, dermatitis herpetiformis, PCP prophylaxis) — overdose or therapeutic accumulation
higher risk in G6PD deficiency
management: High-flow oxygen; IV access; co-oximetry for methaemoglobin; FBC, reticulocytes, LDH, haptoglobin, G6PD where feasible.

Methylene blue ~ 1-2 mg/kg IV slowly for significant/symptomatic methaemoglobinaemia; an infusion (rather than repeated boluses) may better control levels given dapsone's long half-life. Avoid excessive cumulative methylene blue (risk of haemolysis) — generally limit to ~ 2 doses.
Multi-dose activated charcoal — markedly shortens dapsone half-life (reported reduction from ~ 77 h to ~ 13 h) by interrupting enterohepatic recirculation.
Caution: methylene blue may worsen haemolysis and is ineffective/contraindicated in G6PD deficiency — use ascorbic acid / exchange transfusion if needed.
Supportive care; transfuse for severe haemolytic anaemia; admit for prolonged monitoring (rebound methaemoglobinaemia).
antidote: Methylene blue (1-2 mg/kg IV) for methaemoglobinaemia, plus multi-dose activated charcoal to enhance dapsone elimination. Ascorbic acid / exchange transfusion if methylene blue contraindicated.
redFlags: Rebound methaemoglobinaemia hours later — long half-life mandates extended monitoring.
G6PD deficiency — methylene blue ineffective/harmful.
Severe haemolysis — transfusion, supportive care.
High methaemoglobin with end-organ hypoxia.

references.label: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11e — Methemoglobin Inducers (dapsone).
Hall AH et al. Dapsone overdose / methemoglobinemia management. Clinical toxicology literature.

name: Baclofen toxicity
oneLiner: GABA-B agonist overdose: profound CNS depression, respiratory depression, seizures, can mimic brain death — but recovers. No antidote; supportive ICU care. Reinstate baclofen on recovery to prevent dangerous withdrawal.

features.mentalStatus: rapid coma; may appear brain-dead (absent brainstem reflexes) yet recover after 24-48 h
other: withdrawal 24-72 h later if chronic use stopped abruptly

causativeAgents: oral baclofen overdose
intrathecal baclofen pump malfunction / programming error
abrupt withdrawal (especially intrathecal) — distinct, life-threatening syndrome
differentialDiagnosis: structural brain injury / brain death (do NOT diagnose brain death during acute baclofen overdose)
management: ABC; intubate for airway protection/respiratory depression; IV access; continuous monitoring.

Supportive care is the mainstay — there is NO specific antidote; even apparently brain-dead patients may recover after 24-48 h, so do not pursue brain-death determination or organ donation during acute toxicity.
IV fluids ± vasopressors for hypotension; benzodiazepines for seizures; atropine for symptomatic bradycardia.
Activated charcoal if early ingestion AND airway protected.
Reinstate the patient's regular baclofen once recovered — abrupt cessation causes withdrawal (seizures, hallucinations, dyskinesia, autonomic instability) 24-72 h later.
Intrathecal pump problems: involve the implanting team; intrathecal withdrawal may need restoration of intrathecal baclofen, high-dose benzodiazepines, supportive ICU care.
antidote: None — supportive care. Reinstate baclofen on recovery to prevent withdrawal.
redFlags: Apparent brain death during acute overdose — DO NOT conclude brain death; recovery is common.
Respiratory depression / coma — intubate, ICU.
Abrupt baclofen withdrawal (especially intrathecal) — potentially fatal; restore drug urgently.
Refractory seizures.

references.label: Leung NY et al. Baclofen overdose: defining the spectrum of toxicity. Emerg Med Australas 2006.
Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11e — Muscle relaxants (baclofen).

name: Clonidine / imidazoline toxicity
oneLiner: Opioid-mimic toxidrome: miosis + CNS depression + bradycardia + hypotension (transient early hypertension possible). Mostly supportive; naloxone can be tried (often high doses, variable response), atropine for bradycardia.

features.bloodPressure: hypotension (brief paradoxical hypertension may precede it)
features.mentalStatus: lethargy → coma; waxing/waning sedation; arousable with stimulation
other: children especially sensitive (small ingestion can be serious)

causativeAgents: clonidine (oral, transdermal patch ingestion)
other central α2-agonists: guanfacine, tizanidine, dexmedetomidine, methyldopa
imidazoline decongestants: oxymetazoline, tetrahydrozoline, naphazoline (paediatric ingestion)
differentialDiagnosis: opioid overdose (very similar — miosis, CNS/respiratory depression)
management: ABC; airway support / ventilation for respiratory depression; IV access; continuous cardiac monitoring; check glucose.
Supportive care is the mainstay: IV fluids for hypotension (vasopressors e.g. noradrenaline/dopamine if refractory); atropine for symptomatic bradycardia.

Naloxone may reverse CNS/respiratory depression in some patients — response is variable and higher-than-usual doses are often needed (titrated, paediatric dosing 0.1 mg/kg up to 2 mg/dose, repeated); a trial is reasonable given the safety profile.
Do NOT treat the transient early hypertension aggressively — it is short-lived and hypotension follows.
Remove any ingested transdermal patches (including from the GI tract); observe for prolonged effect.
Activated charcoal if early ingestion AND airway protected.
antidote: No definitive antidote; naloxone may help (variable, often high dose). Supportive care, atropine for bradycardia, fluids/vasopressors for hypotension.
redFlags: Children — small ingestions can cause significant toxicity; low threshold to admit.
Apnoea / coma — airway and ventilatory support.
Refractory bradycardia / hypotension.
Transdermal patch ingestion — prolonged, delayed toxicity.

references.label: Seger DL, Loden JK. Naloxone reversal of clonidine toxicity: dose, dose, dose. Clin Toxicol 2018.
Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11e — Clonidine and central-acting antihypertensives.

name: Acute arsenic poisoning
oneLiner: Severe gastroenteritis ('rice-water' diarrhoea) + hypotension + QT prolongation/arrhythmia early; later peripheral neuropathy and pancytopenia. Chelate promptly — DMSA/DMPS preferred; dimercaprol (BAL) for severe acute cases when oral route impossible.

features.skin: later: hyperkeratosis, hyperpigmentation, Mees' lines on nails (chronic/subacute)
features.mentalStatus: encephalopathy, delirium in severe poisoning
features.bowelSounds: profuse vomiting and 'rice-water' diarrhoea; abdominal pain; garlic odour
other: later peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy and pancytopenia

causativeAgents: arsenic trioxide, sodium arsenite/arsenate (pesticides, herbicides, wood preservatives, ant baits)
arsine gas (industrial — predominantly haemolysis)
contaminated water/food, intentional poisoning, some traditional/herbal remedies
management: ABC; aggressive IV fluid resuscitation for GI losses/hypotension; continuous ECG (QT) monitoring; correct potassium/magnesium; treat torsades (magnesium, overdrive pacing).
Confirm with 24-h urinary arsenic (and blood); start treatment on clinical grounds in severe acute poisoning without waiting.

Chelation — begin as early as possible (efficacy falls with delay): oral DMSA (succimer) or DMPS are preferred (water-soluble, less toxic). In severe acute poisoning where the oral route is unreliable (vomiting, shock), use dimercaprol (BAL) by deep IM injection, transitioning to oral DMSA/DMPS when tolerated.
Haemodialysis does not remove arsenic well but is indicated for renal failure (and removes the arsenic-chelate complex in that setting).
Arsine gas exposure: predominantly massive haemolysis → supportive care, exchange transfusion; chelation is of limited value.
antidote: Chelation: DMSA (succimer) or DMPS preferred; dimercaprol (BAL) for severe acute poisoning when oral therapy not feasible. Start early.
redFlags: Hypotension + profuse GI losses — aggressive resuscitation.
Prolonged QT / torsades / ventricular arrhythmia.
Acute kidney injury / haemolysis.
Encephalopathy or evolving neuropathy.

references.label: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11e — Arsenic.
Kosnett MJ. The role of chelation in the treatment of arsenic and mercury poisoning. J Med Toxicol 2013.

name: Lead poisoning (plumbism)
oneLiner: Abdominal pain + anaemia + neuropathy; in children, encephalopathy is the dread complication. Encephalopathy or BLL very high: dimercaprol (BAL) FIRST, then CaNa₂EDTA. Less severe: oral succimer (DMSA).

features.skin: pallor (anaemia); 'lead line' on gums (Burton's line) in chronic exposure
features.mentalStatus: irritability, cognitive impairment; severe (esp. children): encephalopathy, seizures, coma

causativeAgents: occupational (battery, smelting, paint stripping, radiator repair, demolition)
lead-based paint (children — pica), contaminated water, lead-glazed pottery
traditional medicines/cosmetics, contaminated illicit substances, retained lead bullets
differentialDiagnosis: other causes of abdominal pain (acute abdomen)
management: Remove from exposure; identify and abate the source (especially for children).
Check blood lead level (BLL), FBC/blood film, renal function; abdominal X-ray if recent ingestion (radio-opaque foreign body / pica); whole-bowel irrigation for visualised lead in gut.

Encephalopathy or very high BLL (children BLL ≥ 70 µg/dL or encephalopathy; adults symptomatic with high levels): start dimercaprol (BAL) IM FIRST, then CaNa₂EDTA ~ 4 h later — giving EDTA before BAL can redistribute lead into the brain and worsen encephalopathy.
Symptomatic without encephalopathy / children BLL 45-69 µg/dL: oral succimer (DMSA).
Supportive care: control seizures (benzodiazepines), manage cerebral oedema, treat anaemia.
Public-health notification; screen exposed contacts (e.g. household children).
antidote: Chelation: dimercaprol (BAL) FIRST then CaNa₂EDTA for encephalopathy / very high BLL; oral succimer (DMSA) for less severe poisoning.
redFlags: Lead encephalopathy (especially children) — neurological emergency; BAL first, then EDTA.
Giving CaNa₂EDTA before BAL in encephalopathy — can worsen cerebral lead loading.
Seizures / raised intracranial pressure.
Ongoing exposure source not removed — chelation alone fails.

references.label: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11e — Lead.
ATSDR / CDC. Lead toxicity: medical management guidelines.

name: Acute mercury poisoning
oneLiner: Form matters: inhaled elemental Hg vapour → chemical pneumonitis; ingested inorganic Hg salts → corrosive gastroenteritis + acute tubular necrosis. Chelate inorganic/elemental poisoning early with DMSA or DMPS.

features.respiratoryRate: cough, dyspnoea; chemical pneumonitis / ARDS after vapour inhalation
features.skin: metallic taste; later acrodynia (pink, painful extremities) in children
features.mentalStatus: headache, tremor, neuropsychiatric changes
features.bowelSounds: corrosive stomatitis, severe abdominal pain, bloody diarrhoea (inorganic salt ingestion)
other: elemental vapour primarily pulmonary + CNS; inorganic salts primarily GI + renal

causativeAgents: elemental mercury vapour (broken thermometers heated, gold extraction, industrial)
inorganic mercury salts (mercuric chloride) — corrosive, nephrotoxic
organic mercury (methylmercury) — chronic neurotoxicity, NOT effectively chelated the same way
differentialDiagnosis: other causes of corrosive ingestion / AKI
metal fume fever / other inhalational pneumonitis
management: Remove from exposure; staff PPE; supportive care; airway/oxygen for pneumonitis.
Inorganic salt ingestion: aggressive IV fluid resuscitation for shock; do NOT induce emesis; manage as corrosive ingestion; monitor renal function closely.

Chelation for acute inorganic or elemental mercury poisoning — start as early as possible (efficacy declines with delay): DMSA (succimer) or DMPS; dimercaprol (BAL) has been used but is relatively contraindicated for organic (methyl) mercury as it may worsen CNS distribution.
Renal support / haemodialysis for AKI (also removes the chelate complex in renal failure).
Whole-bowel irrigation / careful removal if a large elemental mercury reservoir is ingested (usually low oral bioavailability, but pulmonary aspiration is dangerous).
antidote: Chelation with DMSA (succimer) or DMPS for elemental/inorganic mercury; start early. (Dimercaprol relatively contraindicated for organic mercury.)
redFlags: Severe chemical pneumonitis / ARDS after vapour inhalation.
Corrosive GI injury + shock from inorganic salt ingestion.
Acute kidney injury — may need dialysis.
Do not use BAL for organic (methyl)mercury — worsens CNS distribution.

references.label: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11e — Mercury.
Kosnett MJ. The role of chelation in the treatment of arsenic and mercury poisoning. J Med Toxicol 2013.

name: Paraquat poisoning
oneLiner: Highly lethal herbicide: caustic mucosal burns early, then progressive pulmonary fibrosis and multi-organ failure. NO antidote. Crucially, AVOID supplemental oxygen unless hypoxic (it accelerates lung injury). Early decontamination; specialist/poison-centre advice.

features.respiratoryRate: progressive dyspnoea/tachypnoea as fibrosis develops (often days later)
features.mentalStatus: alert early; deteriorates with multi-organ failure
features.bowelSounds: painful oral/oesophageal ulceration, vomiting, abdominal pain

causativeAgents: paraquat (and the related bipyridyl herbicide diquat) — agricultural herbicide, usually deliberate self-poisoning
differentialDiagnosis: other causes of progressive ARDS / pulmonary fibrosis
management: AVOID supplemental oxygen unless the patient is hypoxic — oxygen generates reactive species that accelerate paraquat-induced lung injury; titrate to lowest acceptable saturations.
Early GI decontamination: activated charcoal (or Fuller's earth) as soon as possible after ingestion — though survival benefit is unproven, reducing absorption is the rationale.
Aggressive IV fluids; monitor renal and hepatic function; manage as a chemical burn for mucosal injury.
Estimate prognosis from plasma paraquat concentration / time and the urine dithionite test; contact a poison centre and specialist toxicology service early.
Immunosuppression (corticosteroids ± cyclophosphamide) and haemoperfusion/haemodialysis have been used but evidence of benefit is weak — under specialist direction only.
Supportive/palliative care for large ingestions where survival is not feasible.
antidote: None. Avoid oxygen unless hypoxic; early decontamination; specialist toxicology / poison-centre guidance.
redFlags: Giving high-flow oxygen routinely — accelerates fatal lung injury; restrict to hypoxia.
Large ingestion (plasma level above the survival line) — usually fatal; involve toxicology early.
Progressive dyspnoea heralding pulmonary fibrosis.
Acute kidney / liver injury.

references.label: Gawarammana IB, Buckley NA. Medical management of paraquat ingestion. Br J Clin Pharmacol 2011.
Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11e — Herbicides (paraquat).

name: Acute ethanol intoxication
oneLiner: CNS depression, ataxia, slurred speech, depressed conscious level; main danger is airway compromise/aspiration and unmasked occult pathology. Supportive care; thiamine before glucose in at-risk patients; always look for co-ingestants and trauma.

features.mentalStatus: disinhibition → ataxia, slurred speech → drowsiness → coma
other: risk of occult head injury masked by intoxication

causativeAgents: ethanol (beverages, hand sanitiser, mouthwash, some colognes)
co-ingestion with sedatives/opioids — synergistic respiratory depression
differentialDiagnosis: toxic alcohols (methanol, ethylene glycol — high osmolar AND anion gap, see those entries)
management: ABC; protect airway (lateral/recovery position; intubate if GCS low / unable to protect airway); the leading risk is aspiration.
Check capillary glucose immediately; treat hypoglycaemia.
Thiamine 100 mg IV before/with glucose in malnourished/alcohol-dependent patients to prevent precipitating Wernicke's encephalopathy.
IV fluids if dehydrated/hypotensive; correct electrolytes; keep warm (treat hypothermia).
Actively search for and treat co-ingestants, trauma (especially head injury), and metabolic mimics — do not attribute all obtundation to alcohol.
No role for routine 'sobering' agents; flumazenil/naloxone only if a specific co-ingestant suspected. Consider toxic-alcohol screen (osmolar/anion gap) if the picture doesn't fit.
antidote: None (no antidote for ethanol itself). Supportive care; thiamine + glucose for hypoglycaemia/Wernicke risk.
redFlags: Depressed conscious level not improving as expected — exclude head injury, hypoglycaemia, toxic alcohols, co-ingestants.
Inability to protect airway — intubate; high aspiration risk.
Hypoglycaemia (children, malnourished).
Raised osmolar/anion gap suggesting methanol or ethylene glycol co-ingestion.

references.label: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11e — Ethanol.
Vonghia L et al. Acute alcohol intoxication. Eur J Intern Med 2008.

name: Colchicine toxicity
oneLiner: Deceptively well early, then catastrophic: GI phase → multi-organ failure/shock/marrow suppression (peak day 2-7) → recovery if survived. NO antidote; doses > 0.8 mg/kg approach 100% mortality. Early charcoal + aggressive ICU support.

features.bloodPressure: hypotension / distributive + cardiogenic shock in systemic phase
features.mentalStatus: alert early; confusion/coma with multi-organ failure
features.bowelSounds: phase 1 (0-24 h): severe vomiting, profuse diarrhoea, abdominal pain, dehydration
other: phase 2 (1-7 days): multi-organ failure, bone-marrow suppression (pancytopenia), shock, rhabdomyolysis, lactic acidosis
phase 3: recovery with rebound leukocytosis and alopecia
lethality: > 0.5-0.8 mg/kg severe, > 0.8 mg/kg near-100% mortality

causativeAgents: colchicine (gout, familial Mediterranean fever) — acute overdose
Colchicum autumnale (autumn crocus) and Gloriosa superba (glory lily) plants
differentialDiagnosis: other causes of multi-organ failure / pancytopenia
management: Recognise that a well-appearing early patient with significant ingestion can deteriorate catastrophically — admit and monitor; estimate dose in mg/kg for risk.
Activated charcoal 1 g/kg if early AND airway protected; multi-dose charcoal may interrupt enterohepatic recirculation.
Aggressive supportive ICU care: fluid resuscitation, vasopressors/inotropes for shock, ventilation for ARDS, correct electrolytes and acidosis.
Treat bone-marrow suppression: G-CSF for neutropenia; transfusion support; broad-spectrum antibiotics for neutropenic sepsis.

There is NO proven antidote (colchicine-specific Fab fragments are not commercially available); haemodialysis does not remove colchicine effectively (large volume of distribution). Plasma exchange/ECMO have been reported as salvage.
Early discussion with poison centre / toxicology.
antidote: None commercially available — supportive ICU care; G-CSF for marrow suppression. (Colchicine-specific Fab is investigational/unavailable.)
redFlags: Ingested dose > 0.5-0.8 mg/kg — anticipate severe/fatal course despite a well-looking patient early.
Transition from GI phase to multi-organ failure (day 1-7).
Pancytopenia / neutropenic sepsis.
Cardiogenic shock / arrhythmia.

references.label: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11e — Colchicine, Podophyllin and the Vinca Alkaloids.
Finkelstein Y et al. Colchicine poisoning: the dark side of an ancient drug. Clin Toxicol 2010.

name: Metformin toxicity / metformin-associated lactic acidosis (MALA)
oneLiner: Severe high-anion-gap lactic acidosis ± hypotension and altered mental status, especially with renal impairment or massive overdose. No antidote; sodium bicarbonate for severe acidosis and early haemodialysis for the sickest (pH ≤ 7.0, lactate > 20, shock).

features.mentalStatus: lethargy → confusion → coma with worsening acidosis
other: hypoglycaemia uncommon with metformin alone (unlike sulfonylureas)

causativeAgents: metformin — acute overdose, or therapeutic use with acute kidney injury / dehydration / sepsis (MALA)
co-ingestants (especially other glucose-lowering agents)
differentialDiagnosis: other causes of high-anion-gap lactic acidosis (sepsis, ischaemia, toxic alcohols, cyanide)
management: ABC; IV access; large-bore; check glucose, lactate, blood gas (pH, anion gap), renal function, electrolytes; continuous monitoring.
Activated charcoal if early presentation after acute overdose AND airway protected.
Aggressive supportive care: IV fluids, vasopressors for shock, treat the precipitant (sepsis, AKI, dehydration).
Sodium bicarbonate infusion for severe acidosis (e.g. pH < 7.1-7.2), particularly with haemodynamic compromise.

Haemodialysis (preferred over CRRT when stable enough; CRRT/sustained therapies if unstable) for severe MALA — EXTRIP criteria: lactate > 20 mmol/L, pH ≤ 7.0, shock, failure of supportive measures, or decreased conscious level. Dialysis removes metformin and lactate and corrects acidosis.
Treat hypoglycaemia if co-ingestant present (metformin alone rarely causes it).
antidote: None — supportive care, sodium bicarbonate for severe acidosis, and early haemodialysis (per EXTRIP criteria) are definitive.
redFlags: pH ≤ 7.0, lactate > 20 mmol/L, shock, or reduced conscious level — urgent haemodialysis.
Acute kidney injury driving metformin accumulation.
Massive ingestion (reported median acute ingestions in grams).
Refractory shock / profound acidosis.

references.label: Calello DP et al. EXTRIP workgroup. Extracorporeal treatment for metformin poisoning. Crit Care Med 2015.
Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11e — Antidiabetics (biguanides).

name: Cardiac glycoside plant poisoning (oleander, foxglove)
oneLiner: Digoxin-like toxidrome from plants: GI upset + bradyarrhythmias/heart block + hyperkalaemia. Digoxin-specific antibody (Fab) fragments rapidly reverse arrhythmias and hyperkalaemia (often higher empiric doses than for digoxin).

features.heartRate: bradycardia, AV block; also ventricular arrhythmias
features.mentalStatus: lethargy, confusion; visual disturbance (xanthopsia) reported
other: hyperkalaemia (marker of severity in acute poisoning)
any dysrhythmia possible (classically bradyarrhythmia/heart block with ectopy)
serum digoxin assay may cross-react but levels do NOT correlate with severity and a negative assay does not exclude plant glycosides

causativeAgents: Nerium oleander and Thevetia peruviana (yellow oleander)
Digitalis purpurea / lanata (foxglove)
lily of the valley (Convallaria), Urginea (squill), and other cardiac-glycoside-containing plants
differentialDiagnosis: other causes of bradyarrhythmia / heart block (beta-blocker, calcium-channel blocker, ACS)
management: ABC; continuous cardiac monitoring; IV access; check potassium and renal function; 12-lead ECG.
Activated charcoal if early AND airway protected; multi-dose charcoal has been used (interrupts enterohepatic recirculation, e.g. in yellow-oleander poisoning).

Digoxin-specific antibody (Fab) fragments for life-threatening dysrhythmias, haemodynamic instability, or significant hyperkalaemia — they rapidly reverse oleander/foxglove toxicity; because levels don't correlate, empiric (often larger) dosing is guided by clinical severity.
Atropine for symptomatic bradycardia; temporary pacing if needed (use cautiously).

Manage hyperkalaemia supportively; correct hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia which potentiate toxicity. (Caution with IV calcium in cardiac-glycoside hyperkalaemia — traditionally avoided; treat the toxicity with Fab.)
Treat ventricular arrhythmias (e.g. lidocaine, magnesium); avoid agents that worsen conduction.
antidote: Digoxin-specific antibody (Fab) fragments — rapidly reverse cardiac glycoside plant toxicity; dose empirically by clinical severity (levels unreliable).
redFlags: Hyperkalaemia in acute poisoning — marker of severe toxicity; give Fab.
High-grade AV block / bradyarrhythmia / ventricular arrhythmia.
Haemodynamic instability.
Do not rely on a serum digoxin level to grade plant-glycoside severity.

references.label: Eddleston M et al. Anti-digoxin Fab fragments in cardiotoxicity induced by yellow oleander poisoning. Lancet 2000.
Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11e — Cardioactive Steroids.

name: Caustic (corrosive) ingestion — acid / alkali
oneLiner: Alkalis cause liquefactive oesophageal injury; acids cause coagulative gastric injury. Do NOT induce emesis, give charcoal, or 'neutralise' (exothermic). Secure airway; early endoscopy (12-24 h) to grade injury.

features.respiratoryRate: stridor / respiratory distress with airway injury or aspiration
features.mentalStatus: usually alert; distressed by pain
features.bowelSounds: odynophagia, dysphagia, drooling, retrosternal/epigastric pain, vomiting (sometimes haematemesis)
other: risk of oesophageal/gastric perforation, mediastinitis, peritonitis
late oesophageal strictures; long-term oesophageal cancer risk

causativeAgents: alkalis: drain/oven cleaners (sodium/potassium hydroxide), dishwasher detergents, ammonia, button batteries, bleach (usually milder)
acids: toilet-bowl/rust removers, descalers (hydrochloric, sulfuric), some pool chemicals
differentialDiagnosis: hydrofluoric acid (special systemic toxicity — see separate entry)
foreign body / button battery (impaction with rapid burn)
other causes of acute dysphagia / chest pain
management: ABC — airway is the priority: assess for stridor/hoarseness/oedema; early intubation (ideally awake/fibreoptic) by experienced clinician before swelling progresses; have surgical airway backup.
Do NOT induce vomiting, do NOT give activated charcoal (doesn't bind, obscures endoscopy), and do NOT attempt chemical neutralisation (exothermic reaction worsens injury).
Nil by mouth; IV fluids; analgesia; antiemetics; PPI commonly given.
Upright positioning; avoid blind nasogastric tube insertion.
Upper GI endoscopy within ~ 12-24 h (up to ~ 48 h) to grade injury and prognosticate; AVOID endoscopy in the ~ 5-15 day window (highest perforation risk). CT chest/abdomen if perforation suspected.
Surgery for perforation/transmural necrosis; involve GI/surgery/ENT early; monitor for late stricture; consider ophthalmology/dermatology for associated external burns.
antidote: None — supportive care; airway protection and endoscopic grading are central. Neutralisation and charcoal are contraindicated.
redFlags: Airway compromise (stridor, hoarseness, drooling) — secure airway early.
Signs of perforation / mediastinitis / peritonitis — surgical emergency.
Button battery in oesophagus — rapid burn; emergency removal.
Attempts at neutralisation / emesis / charcoal — contraindicated and harmful.

references.label: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies, 11e — Caustics.
Hoffman RS et al. Ingestion of caustic substances. N Engl J Med 2020;382:1739-1748.
